speakeroldname: Hon. W. G. Dinsdale (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: ARCTIC ISLANDS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF DRILLING OF EXPLORATORY WELL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce that a well in search of oil and gas will be drilled in the Arctic islands this year. This is the first exploratory well to test this major northern sedimentary basin, one of the last great untested potential oil and gas producing basins in the world. The decision to commence drilling operations follows two years of broad scale geological work in the Arctic islands.
90205-6-402
The project represents an outstanding example of initiative on the part of private enterprise in Canada. The necessary capital has been raised by Dome Petroleum Limited on a co-operative basis. This investment under the leadership of a Canadian company in the development of our resources is an encouraging response to the government's program of northern development, and suggests that the recent amendments to the oil and gas regulations have had a beneficial effect.
There are many difficulties to be overcome, not the least of which is transportation. The drilling rig will be loaded on freight cars in Calgary to be shipped to Montreal. From there it will be transshipped to a freighter which will take it to the islands during this summer's shipping season. Depending on ice conditions, drilling will take place in the high Arctic on either Melville island or Bathurst island.
Oil and gas exploration in the north is now entering a new phase. Should success result from this first venture, it will be the first of many wells to be drilled in the islands and will mark the beginning of a new era in the economy of Canada's Arctic. I am sure that Canadians everywhere will watch the operation with keen interest.

Supply-Public Works

speechtext:
At least the Postmaster General agrees with that statement. We have been working with him for a long time, however. In 1961-62 the department expects to do a substantial volume of construction work for other departments using funds from their appropriations. On the basis of present information, 470 projects in this category are expected to be carried out for 15 other departments with a total expenditure in 1961-62 estimated at $37|- million. Some of them are new and others are to be continued from 1960-61. The larger projects in this category will be of interest to hon. members, and I will summarize them briefly. In other words, this is work outside the Department of Public Works, and outside what we would ordinarily do in the past.
Department of Agriculture: a science service laboratory at Vancouver.
Department of Citizenship and Immigration: a large number of schools and residences, including a school at Pointe Bleue agency, Quebec; hostels at Whitehorse; a residential school at Mission, B.C.; a school at Pelly agency, Saskatchewan, and a water supply system at Fort George, James bay agency.
Department of Fisheries: construction of several community fishing stages in Newfoundland; a gear research Laboratory at Nanaimo, B.C.; a workshop building at St. Andrews, N.B.; and conversion of the electrical system at biological station in Nanaimo, B.C.
Department of Forestry: a garage and oflice building at Quebec city.
Department of Mines and Technical Surveys: construction of the Bedford institute at Bedford basin, Dartmouth, N.S. and road construction at Victoria, B.C.
Department of National Defence: reconstruction of the jetty at Esquimalt, B.C.; reconstruction of a naval radio station at Inuvik;

repairs to the jetty at Patricia Bay, B.C.; and repairs to the fuel oil depot at Colwood, B.C.
National research council: communications laboratory building at Riverside drive, Ottawa, and applied physics building at Montreal road.
Department of National Health and Welfare: a hospital at Inuvik, N.W.T.; a hospital at Whitehorse, Y.T.; a nursing station at Habay, Alberta; repair of civil defence building at Arnprior.
Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources: large contracts for highway construction, other than trans-Canada, in the national parks-Banff, Kootenay, Cape Breton, Prince Edward Island and Yoho; a school and hostel at Fort Simpson, Northwest Territories; road reconstruction in the Yukon, on the Keno road at Whitehorse and on the Flat Creek-Eagle Plain road. In addition, a survey and some new construction will be undertaken on the road from Watson Lake to Ross. In the Northwest Territories, road work will be undertaken on the Mackenzie highway from Frank Channel to Rae, and on the road from Yellowknife to McKay Lake.
For the R.C.M.P., for which my colleague the Minister of Justice is responsible, a large number of detachment quarters are to be built, among them buildings at Queen Charlotte, British Columbia; Carmacks, Yukon Territory; Summerside, Prince Edward Island; Grand Manan, New Brunswick; Shelburne, Nova Scotia; Lillooet, British Columbia and Rock Island, Quebec.
For the Department of Transport the program includes marine agency buildings at Saint John, New Brunswick, and St. John's, Newfoundland; wharf and sheds at Corner Brook and Lewisporte, Newfoundland; work on the Toronto island airport and dredging at Cape Tormentine, New Brunswick.
For the Department of Veterans Affairs the program includes a therapeutic wing at the Shaughnessy hospital, Vancouver; a laundry at Ste. Anne de Bellevue, and a new hospital wing in London, Ontario.
I wish to thank the ministers in charge of these various departments of government for their complete co-operation in entrusting to the Department of Public Works so many important projects. I have outlined to the committee only the highlights of the department's work program. I know that hon. members will have questions to ask concerning individual items which are of particular interest to them and about which they may require additional information from me. I shall be glad to give them all the information I can at this time.

Finally, since I understand some hon. members are concerned about this, I can assure the committee that I feel very good natured today.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) for the information he has just given us. It will prove useful, I expect, for the discussion that will follow.
I was glad to hear him say a moment ago that he is fully willing to discuss matters related to his department.
He realizes, I suppose, that since he has been Minister of Public Works, he often loses his temper. I hope that in this debate, he will manage to contain himself so that the discussion will be intelligent and serious.
I was somewhat surprised by the brevity of his remarks on the activities of his department. He is usually more talkative. He certainly has no reason to be, especially where the accomplishments of the government or his department are concerned.
I think I understand him on that point because ever since he took charge of the Department of Public Works, both activities and expenditures have been decreasing year after year.
(Text):

Shame, Shame.
(Translation):

As last year, I will limit my remarks to general observations and then add to them as each item is considered separately.
As in the past, I should have liked to make an analysis by using charts to show what percentage of the appropriations were actually used during the last fiscal year, namely 1960-61.
That would have enabled us to better appreciate the efficiency of the department during the past year.
These analyses showed that in 1958-59, the expenditures amounted to 89.5 per cent of the appropriations, while they amounted to 90 per cent in 1959-60.
For 1960-61, in view of the fact that the estimates of the department are being examined before the budget speech, it is impossible to make such an analysis, since we lack the required data, which are contained in papers tabled by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) when he introduces the budget.
It seems appropriate however to bring to the attention of the members of the committee the fact that during the current year, the number of unemployed reached a record percentage, that is 11.3 per cent of the labour
Supply-Public Works
force in February 1961. Yet this government, which advocated full employment and whose leader had said that no one would suffer because of unemployment, had requested for the Department of Public Works appropriations exceeding by only $7.9 million the amounts voted for 1956-57, the last year of the former administration.
This amount of $7.9 million does not include, of course, amounts provided for the construction of the trans-Canada highway, which are statutory expenses depending upon the activity of the provinces.
Thus I had every reason to say, as we have every right to repeat now, that there has been a reversal of the policy that the government was supposed to lay down, since it has renounced its famous public works program which was to supply jobs for everyone.
As I pointed out last year, if you analyse the estimates of the Minister of Public Works for the years 1958-59, 1959-60 and 1960-61, you find that instead of going up, as was the case under the Liberal administration, the expenses of the department have steadily declined from year to year. In 1958-59, expenditures ran to a total of $220 million whereas for the year 1959-60, the total was only $203.8 million. Finally, for the year just ended, we had been asked to vote $195.9 million including expenses for the trans-Canada highway, a decrease of $25 million in relation to the previous year. Under the Liberal administration, the amounts voted showed an increase every year, going from $37.2 million in 1946-47 to $147.5 million for the year 1956-57.
Last year, when these estimates came up, I asked the minister whether he could justify the fact that there had been such a drop in the work of the department at a time when unemployment was reaching alarming heights and when future prospects were none too bright. Here was the minister's reply, as recorded on page 6619 of Hansard for July 20, 1960:
The hon. member for Levis asked me why we cut $25 million from last year's public works budget. There are two reasons. The first reason is, of course, that in the two previous years, in an effort to get out of the recession, a great spending program, although a proper and well directed spending program, was initiated. It was felt that this could not be kept up forever and that it was a very good thing to cut back this year because we had hopes of having a very prosperous year and, aside from the unemployment figures, the gross national product is going to be exceptionally good.

Supply-Public Works
The minister went on to say:
As my hon. friend also knows, when the Minister of Finance made his budget address the hon. member for Levis was one of those who voted for a balanced budget. I am not always in favour of the suggestions made by the Minister of Finance. Sometimes we are at odds. Naturally, all the backbenchers are on my side because they want things X am convinced they should have. Sometimes I have to bow to the Minister of Finance and you are quite right when you suggest that.
At that point, I reminded the minister that he was forgetting the promises made in 1957 and 1958. Here is his reply:
Hon. members not only got promises, but they got results. The benefits of a balanced budget are obvious, even to my engineering friend the hon. member for Levis. I do not need to go into that. What would have happened in the country so far as finance is concerned? We have to have our financial institutions operating properly if we want to have business operating as well as possible. I need not go into that.
Indeed, Mr. Chairman, it was better at the time for the minister not to go into that, and I feel sure that when he is reminded today of the statements he made last July, he wishes he had never made them, because they were just another vision or dream that never came true.
The Minister of Public Works was at that time completely in error. I have shown a moment ago on the basis of statistics that the amounts spent by the Department of Public Works, instead of rising as should be the case in view of the fact that the expenses of the department should expand along with the development of the Canadian nation, have been steadily dropping since 1958-59.
This is why I say that the extensive public works program which we heard so much about has never existed except in the minds of government supporters, in spite of the goodly number of unemployed that kept increasing from year to year.
Moreover, I suggest that the prediction about the tremendous increase in the gross national product has proved altogether false, since the 6 per cent rise expected by the Minister of Finance reached only 3.2 per cent, or 2.1 per cent, if price increases are taken into account.
As far as the matter of a balanced budget is concerned, the minister must agree with us today that he was entirely wrong since the expected budget surplus of $12 million has turned into a deficit of almost $300 million.
[Mr. Bourget.l
I recognize, of course, Mr. Chairman, that a balanced budget has certain advantages. But, in spite of all their promises, did we have any balanced budgets since the Conservatives came into power? No, not even one. On the contrary, we had an uninterrupted series of deficits now exceeding $2 billion. That is why our country finds itself in a bad financial situation, the interest on the national debt is going up in a frightening way, the interest rates are prohibitive and our manufacturers, businessmen, workers and farmers find it difficult to borrow money. It is also because of the lack of action and foresight on the part of the government and the absence of any well conceived and orderly plans that we have today 700,000 unemployed in Canada.
Therefore, we have a right to say that the government has failed in its duty, that it is proceeding in a fog toward an unknown destination.
The minister also stated that he was not always in agreement with the suggestions of the Minister of Finance and that sometimes he had to give in to him. Then, how can he reconcile his remarks with what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) himself said as recorded on page 3569 of Hansard for January 21, 1958, and I quote:
While next year we would unquestionably like to have a balanced budget, let me make it abundantly clear that we are not going to put a balanced budget above our firm determination to provide, through the agency of public works, jobs for unemployed Canadians.
I would then advise the minister to remind the Minister of Finance of those words when he has to justify his department's appropriations before the treasury board. Then, he will not have to give in to him or to give reasons which do not stand by themselves to justify his conduct.
Mr. Chairman, I should now like to analyse briefly the estimates for the fiscal year 1961-62. I say briefly because they are neither numerous nor impressive. We are asked to vote an amount of $166,548,544, that is only $2.3 million more than last year's vote.
On the other hand, if we subtract from those appropriations $2.7 million for the national capital commission which came under the privy council until last year, we find that the Department of Public Works' appropriations were, in fact, again

reduced this year by some $400,000. In other words, they are $25.4 million less than for the fiscal year 1959-60.
Incidentally, I should like to point out, Mr. Chairman, that this amount of $25.4 million is about the equivalent of the government's appropriations for the winter works program, which bring me to the conclusion that what the government gives us with one hand, they take away with the other.
Who said that?

By analysing the two major services, that is the one which looks after the construction, acquisition, maintenance and improvement of public buildings and the harbours and rivers engineering services, I find that, in the first case, appropriations have been pared by $5,447,000 whereas in the second case, they were increased by $3,558,000. In other words, appropriations for the two major services of the department have been cut down by nearly $2 million.
This year again, I would like the minister to give us the reasons for such a decrease in his estimates, when unemployment is known to be increasing, year after year. Is he trying to help the Minister of Finance balance his budget, as he said last year? He should then put an end to all expenditures, cut all building projects in his department, for if the experts are right, the deficit for the current fiscal year will be twice as high as that predicted for 1960-61. Or is it that the department is short of projects?
Yet the minister's predecessor said in the house on June 6, 1958, that he was going to have a reserve of public works to be undertaken on short notice. Where are those projects? Where are they? Is the reserve already depleted? Is the minister feeling tired? Or are the projects being kept for an election year?
I could easily, Mr. Chairman, point out a few to the minister that could be undertaken immediately and could even have been undertaken last year if the department had seen to it.
As a matter of fact, in the department's estimates for 1959-60, a sum of $600,000 was earmarked for the construction of a building in Quebec city for an unemployment insurance office there. Nothing has been done so far, except that the old hospital has been demolished.
Supply-Public Works
Last year, another amount of $500,000 was provided for the same purpose, and nothing has been done.
I then asked the minister why construction had not been started. He answered that the accommodation committee looking into this matter had needed time to decide if the building would house only the unemployment insurance commission or several government services. He added that the committee had settled the problem and that the building would only be used to accommodate unemployment insurance. Well, that was in July last year and nothing has been done so far.
Another item of $575,000 is provided again this year for the construction of that building. If the same eagerness is shown this year as in the last two years, I can guarantee that nothing will be done. I even wonder if the plans have even been started. If not, it will take at least five to six months to complete the plans and specifications, a month and a half for the calling of tenders and another month to consider the tenders and award the contract. That means that even if the plans were started immediately, actual work could not begin before the end of this fiscal year.
And yet, the minister has certainly not forgotten that when visiting Quebec in January 1960-i.e. a year and a half ago- he announced the site where the building was to be erected and said that $500,000 had been provided in the last estimates for that construction. His parliamentary secretary and representative for the riding was present. Unfortunately the Quebec East constituents are still waiting. They may find some consolation, however, in the fact that they are not the only ones waiting for this government to honor its promises.
Indeed, in the city of Toronto where the minister lives, construction of a building to accommodate unemployment insurance had been announced in the 1959-60 estimates. It was supposed to be erected at the corner of Dundas and Jarvis streets and $400,000 had been voted for that purpose.
I want to point out that this was another building to house unemployment insurance. And accommodation for that department is badly needed under the Tories because they have so many unemployed.

Supply-Public Works
Well, the following year, that is in 1960-61, the same amount of $400,000 was voted again for the very same building. And this year, we are asked to vote $900,000.
Now, on February 22 last, I put a starred question asking whether the plans and specifications of the Toronto unemployment insurance office were ready. The minister's parliamentary secretary answered as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to this question is that it was originally expected that the plans and specifications would be completed by April 1, 1961. A basic change in the accommodation requirements has been proposed, and until this has been dealt with it is not possible to say when the plans and specifications will be completed.
That is another project for which we have been called upon to vote estimates for two years and a half and they do not know yet when the plans will be completed.
Surely, you cannot expect the hon. members of the committee to believe that during that long period, it could not have been possible to have the plans completed and the building started. Well, either they do not want the project carried out now or there is carelessness. The delay in carrying out that project cannot be explained otherwise.
The minister seems to be in need of suggestions about new projects the department would like to carry out. Well, I should like to make a very interesting suggestion which, I hope, will meet the approval not only of the minister but also of all hon. members, whether they sit on this side or on the other side of the house.
We know that, in Ottawa, the capital of this country, many conventions are held and that, unfortunately, there is no suitable building or local for that type of meeting. Since in six years from now, that is in 1967, we will celebrate the 100th anniversary of the Canadian confederation, would it not be wise to consider, right now, the possibility of erecting a federal building which might be used for that purpose and which, at the same time, could be considered as a monument erected in our capital properly to mark that important event in the life of our country?
Furthermore, I suggest that all provinces get together with regard to that project, in the sense that the name of each be given to one of the halls of the building.
Hear, hear.

The minister could at the same time take the opportunity to organize a competition open to all Canadian architects. I

am sure they would be only too glad to cooperate to a project of such scope. I do not intend to say any more about that project for the time being, but I think this suggestion should be seriously considered by the minister and his officials.
And now, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words about the possibility of building a causeway that would cross Northumberland strait to link New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
As all members of the committee, I noticed that in the remarks he made this morning and yesterday the minister had nothing to say about that important project which has been under consideration for four years.
Last year, on the discussion of these estimates, I mentioned a number of studies carried out by various government departments and firms of consulting engineers. I also pointed out to the minister that in my opinion with that data available the approximate cost of the project could be estimated so that it could be determined whether it was economically feasible or not. I added that studies and research in the future would affect only in a small way the estimate of cost for the project.
Later on, in the same debate, I asked the minister when he expected to be in receipt of a final report on the feasibility of that project, or when he expected the termination of research carried out by the national research council to ascertain whether this project was economically feasible. Here is the answer the minister gave me. I quote:
This week, the N.B.C. told us they hoped the results would be available next fall. As soon as possible afterward-
It is always as soon as possible.
-we shall decide whether the work is feasible and we will then be in a position to give a definite answer to the hon. member as to the total cost of the project.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I feel that after three and even four years of study, which cost almost $700,000, members of the committee, and particularly the public in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, have a right to know whether the project is feasible and what the government intends to do in that regard.
I hope the minister will make up his mind and tell us exactly what the situation is, now that the by-election has been held in Prince Edward Island, because after four years of consideration-and I repeat-after

expenditures of $700,000, we have a right to know what are the intentions of the government about that important project.
Mr. Chairman, may I now-

Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend from Essex East (Mr. Martin) says that he entirely agrees with me.
Mr. Chairman, I now come to the program for the construction of smaller post offices in some communities. The minister knows that the program was approved by all hon. members and that the citizens want those post offices in many places.
In 1960 and 1961, I received from two municipalities in my riding, that is St. Lambert and St. Louis de Pintendre, requests for small post offices in those two municipalities. I then referred those requests to the Post Office Department and to the Department of Public Works with the reasons which, in my opinion, could justify the departments to agree to them. Later, I received very polite answers saying that those two post offices were of the class called revenue post offices and that in those cases, the quarters were usually provided by the local postmasters.
I have no criticism in the case of the request from St. Lambert parish, for the revenues of that office in 1959-1960 were only $2,076.54, or almost $1,000 less than the required amount of $3,000, according to the information given to me last year by the minister.
Supply-Public Works
However, I fail to understand why the St. Louis de Pintendre request was turned down by the minister, because, according to the Post Office Department publication "List of Post Offices with revenues", that office's revenues in 1959-60 reached $3,411.23. Besides, I am convinced that there is just as much work to do in that post office as in others that have been built by the government under this policy.
I know from experience that it is difficult to grant all requests during the same year, but I think that if they meet the required standards, they should be granted even if construction has to be deferred until the next year. The municipalities concerned would then feel that they are all being; treated in the same manner.
Unless there are reasons that I am not aware of, I ask the minister to reconsider his decision on the request of St. Louis de Pintendre so that the citizens of that municipality may feel they are given the same treatment as those in other municipalities.
And while I am on the subject of small post offices, I would like to draw the minister's attention to the general appearance of the post offices built in recent years.
Members of the committee will recall that in May I told the house about the complaints of the population and public organizations of Rouyn, in the province of Quebec, about the drab appearance of this town's new post office building.
The following day, the minister replied that he had received the particular complaints and that the department would improve the looks of the building by the removal of a construction shack and the contractor's signs. He added that efflorescence on the brickwork would be removed and a general cleaning up around the building would be carried out.
You do not have to be an architect or an engineer to realize that the minister paid little attention to the complaints of the people involved, because otherwise, his reply would have been different.
The complaints made in the circumstances had nothing to do with the normal cleaning up job to be done after a building is completed. As I have indicated, they referred to the disgraceful appearance of the building itself, in other words to its exterior design, its architectural design.
Foundations had been laid, then a floor and after that four walls had been set up and a roof put on top. But no attention had been paid the building's architectural design, in order to make it attractive.
I hope there is no need to belabour the point. I am sure the minister, and particularly the officials of his department, know what I

Supply-Public Works
mean. I also hope that in the future we will hear no more such complaints, and even if it costs a few thousand dollars more to the government, I hope they will be spent, so that the municipalities may be proud of their public buildings.
The last point I wish to discuss briefly-I shall refer to it again when the relevant item comes up-concerns the trans-Canada highway.
At long last, after 11 years of waiting caused by the stubborn refusal of the Conservative government in the province of Quebec, a Liberal government has been elected to office in that province and an agreement has been reached on this highway.
That agreement between the federal government and the provincial government was signed on October 29, 1960.
For a period of 11 years, the late government of the Union Nationale had refused the benefits of this plan under the fallacious pretext that this project was altogether unacceptable and inconsistent with provincial autonomy. I may even go on to say that the great majority of Conservative members from the province of Quebec now sitting in this house supported the views of the late great leader of the Union Nationale. But now they do not utter a word. In their opinion, this project does not now infringe upon any aspect of provincial autonomy, probably because it is introduced by a Conservative government.
This 11 years of stubborn refusal has cost the province of Quebec millions of dollars-
Shame.

It is difficult to estimate the exact amount so lost, but I can say that a considerable part of the Montreal metropolitan boulevard, which will cost almost $130 million, could have been paid by the federal government. It is thus easier to see now that such stubbornness on the part of the previous provincial administration was most costly.
Some time ago the hon. member for Mont-magny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin) put a question to the Minister of Public Works. He wanted to know whether the Department of Public Works intended to pay part of the metropolitan boulevard under the trans-Canada highway program.
He apparently was happy to hear the minister say that he would not pay that part which was built before an agreement was entered into by the federal and provincial governments.
I regret that an hon. member from the province of Quebec has put such a question to the minister, for I know that his intention was to say that Mr. Lesage-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Answering the hon. member for Levis, as he asks this specific question, may I say that the average expenditure by Department of Public Works from 1945 until we took over in 1957 was $90 million a year. Since we took over the average has been $218 million a year. For the Department of Public Works and other departments for the period under the Liberals from the war until the Conservative party took power, the average was $109 million a year and under the Conservatives it has been $234 million a year. That is the answer to the allegation that we have cut down on public works.
You certainly have cut down.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
We have increased them by 113 per cent in our own department without any of the other work that we are doing for other departments. I do not want to engage in any controversy, because I am not in the mood for it. However, these are just some of the facts.

Supply-Public Works

If the minister would look at the figures that appear in the blue book I think he would realize that since 1959, since he has taken over as Minister of Public Works, the estimates of his department have been going down. I said the situation was contrary to that under the previous administration. I have here the estimates of the department from 1946-47 to 1957-58. If the minister would like to have a copy I will give it to him, so he will be able to see that the situation was different under the Liberal administration. Even last year the minister himself admitted-and this admission can be found in Hansard-that the estimates of his department had gone down $25 million. That he cannot deny. He admitted it himself.

Speaking for this group I wish to make a few non-partisan and objective observations on the activities of our multi-use minister and his multilateral department. The scope of the minister's activities is really remarkable. Not only is he Minister of Public Works; he is the minister responsible for the activities of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I found out that he had also been the curator of a miniature art gallery on behalf of the people of Canada, unknown to himself. I now find that he is also custodian of the red carpet for this government. I discovered that fact quite lately. I am always interested in the scope of the minister's activities.
Before proceeding I wish to say that I understand that the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is one of the members for Halifax, usually warms up the minister's audiences when he visits the maritimes. It might have been a nice gesture if he had made a sort of introductory speech on the minister's estimates in order to excite or warm us up a bit. However, possibly that is not necessary in view of the furor displayed in the last few minutes.
I was pleased to listen to the review by the minister of the building activities of the department, of the buildings that are being built in the country and of the proposals for certain buildings at headquarters in Ottawa. I must say that this group is particularly interested to hear of plans for the commencement of a national library building. This has been advocated by a good many members in this House of Commons and others and we are very pleased to hear it.
I must say this, and in this respect I think I am speaking generally for the members of our group. We appreciate the minister's courtesy when dealing with representations made to him by various members, and his prompt attention to those representations. Whether or not he is successful, it is rather heartening to a member to have a minister undertake to

look into the question and give him a prompt and complete reply with respect to all these circumstances. We also appreciate his readiness to discuss even small problems that are brought to his attention in connection with his department. I also wish to express our appreciation of the attitude and the approach of the deputy minister, the senior staff in Ottawa and the district staffs throughout the country.
In connection with staffs I want to make two observations. As far as the professional technical and trained staffs are concerned, I hope their salaries are in line with the salaries being paid by private industry to persons performing the same type of service. I have had brought to my attention on one or two occasions in British Columbia recently instances in which we have lost extremely good men because private industry made them very attractive offers. In order to maintain the efficiency of the department I think the salaries of technical and professional personnel must be in line with those paid by private industry.
I have one other matter to mention in respect to men employed on public works contracts throughout the country. I think there must be a little stricter policing of the fair wages clauses of the contracts signed by various contractors. No doubt the labour department supplies the Department of Public Works with information as to the prevailing rates and the circumstances in any particular community. However, I suggest that a very close watch be kept upon contractors, under certain circumstances, in order to make sure they are paying the prevailing rates and that the working conditions are those accepted in the area in which the work is being done.
Another thing I wish to mention is this. I understand that under these contracts a contractor undertakes to engage, as far as possible, local labour. I have noticed a few cases in which the bulk of the labour-and I am speaking of circumstances within my own knowledge-were employees who came from the coastal area into the interior while there were men in the community, carpenters and other artisans, who were quite capable of doing the work. I can understand the need for bringing in certain supervisory personnel. However, I think the department must watch this aspect of contracts more closely than it has been watched in the past.
I understand the difficulties. District officers must depend upon correspondence, and the administrative staff is some distance from these operations in isolated and smaller communities. In this respect I suggest that it would be a good idea to ask the inspector or the clerk of works, as I think he is properly

called, to inform the department of the number of local persons who are employed and the number of imported personnel. I think the clerk of works on the job could keep the district architect informed of any particular violations.
We are very pleased to note that it is increasingly the policy of the Department of Public Works to undertake the greater part of the construction work for the government of Canada. That is a very changed situation compared with the situation of only a few years ago, when I think most of the outside work undertaken by the department was for the Post Office Department. I think it is an excellent development. It will add to efficiency and give some continuity to the approach of government toward public construction, and provide for the building up of an efficient and satisfactory staff instead of having pockets of staff in various departments concerned particularly with the construction of buildings and projects of that type. I think the present policy has been proven wise by results.
In this connection I cannot resist quoting briefly from an item in the Ottawa Journal of Saturday, May 13, which touches on this point. I think it deals with the subject very well:
Another feather in the efficiency hat of the public works department has been the decision to have it take over the architectural and engineering branch of the penitentiaries commission from the Justice department.
It was only seven years ago that public works built only for the Post Office Department, and, of course, took care of its own construction.
Now it's the builder for every federal department and agency except national defence and transport, and even for those it does all but the big basic construction jobs.
I endorse wholeheartedly the sentiments expressed in that item, and I suggest that the Department of National Defence, from my knowledge of certain circumstances, would save a lot of money if they let the Department of Public Works build their buildings from now on. I must say this all demonstrates that the minister and his officials are applying the principles of socialist planning to the operations of the Department of Public Works and that is why we in this group are so pleased with the purpose and activities of this department.
I have a few other suggestions to make. My remarks at this stage will be directed mainly to administration, but later on I shall have some more parochial comments to make on the appropriate items. One other suggestion I have is this. I think it would be a good idea if the minister found an opportunity to travel more than he does to various parts of the country. I know he is a very busy person, but I think his presence would
Supply-Public Works
be welcomed at outside points. I know it would in the Kootenays; we would give him a rousing welcome, as we do all prominent persons. But we see so few of them. The minister goes to Vancouver, spends a day or so with his officials there and drives around the city, but how rarely does either he or other ministers come into the southeastern interior. I do suggest he should find an opportunity to do that.
The same applies to the deputy minister. I think there is nothing like seeing the projects on the ground and the country in which the department is carrying on its activities in order to understand the local problems and difficulties. I suggest that more of that be done wherever possible. But even if it is limited, for heaven's sake let us have a visit from the minister or the deputy minister at least once in ten years in the southeastern portion of British Columbia.
With respect to the staff in British Columbia, I am a great believer in decentralization in administration and, as you know, in the southeastern part of British Columbia and in the Kootenays particularly there has been tremendous development. We had a very busy period in the early days of this century, when we had a district engineer and an assistant district engineer, who had a palatial boat and used to arrive in style at all the smaller places. Over the years the steamers disappeared and there was a certain stability, shall I say, in population and activity. But the area is now developing very quickly indeed with the expansion of the mining and smelting industry and the forest industry.
I have been asked to mention this by various chambers of commerce, business people and community organizations whose members are long time residents who remember the early days and are interested in future developments. We suggest there should be a district engineer living in the southeastern portion of British Columbia. There is more work to be done, and I think an engineer needs to live in a district in order to understand the circumstances which arise particularly with respect to rivers, waters, erosion, floods, local building conditions and other local circumstances.
I have been asked to bring this to the attention of the minister and suggest that it might be appropriate as soon as possible to have a district engineer responsible for the southern interior living in the southern interior, instead of him finding it necessary to come from Vancouver periodically to make a hurried visit to the district. There is nothing like getting the feel of the district and a knowledge of the people, and also belonging to certain of the local organizations in order

Supply-Public Works
to gain closer contact, appreciation and understanding of district problems and requirements.
Because of these recent developments I have another suggestion to make. I think there has been a bit of slackness in this regard both on the part of the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport throughout the years. I should like the minister to tell us, when he can find time-I do not expect an early reply-how many complaints he has received from any officials in the last 50 years with respect to violations of the provisions of the Navigable Waters Protection Act in so far as they affect the responsibility of the Minister of Public Works. I intended to ask the Minister of Transport the same question.
These things were not serious years ago. People would drive piles without permission and string booms without permission. They would dump sawdust into our lakes, and it would go unobserved and unreported. I do suggest that because of the development which has taken place, in order to prevent the pollution of our rivers and the dumping of slabs and logs and things of that sort, the officials responsible should be told to watch carefully for any improper driving of piles or any improper stringing of booms and to make certain that saw mills-there are very few offenders in this respect-are not dumping their slabs into the river. I am not sure where the division of responsibility lies. I mentioned this when the estimates of the Minister of Transport were before the committee, and I mention it again now so the minister may consider just what aspect of this question comes under his jurisdiction.
I must say I read the annual report. You know, I am interested in public works. It is the sort of concrete subject that a simple mind like mine can understand. I am not much on the abstract art they have down at the national gallery, but I do know what a wharf is and what a highway is, or a building, and I must say that the annual report reflects the spirit of organized purpose which has been developed in this department since Mr. Winters took over as minister. That was the time when there was a change in direction in the administration of this department. I found the report informing, and the explanation of the activity of each branch and division interesting. The details are clear and understandable.
I am interested in knowing what is being done with respect to appropriate designs for public buildings. I mentioned this last year at somewhat greater length. Are competitions held? I am interested in the design of public buildings, and for this reason I should like the minister to tell the committee what the

policy is in this regard. The smaller buildings are, I think, most suitable and attractive; the smaller post offices and R.C.M.P. buildings, for example. They are generally appreciated through the country, and there are many favourable comments.
However, I do not see any definite policy with respect to the design of the larger buildings to the end that when you go into a city you will know that certain buildings have been built by the federal Department of Public Works, buildings which are not only functional but which are attractive to look at as well. I should like the minister to tell us what is the policy with respect to the design of public buildings, particularly the larger ones, and also what is the policy with respect to air conditioning in federal buildings. I think air conditioning is very necessary in Ottawa and it is necessary, also, in some other points throughout the country, particularly in the larger buildings.
Then I should like him to tell me what the policy is with respect to the administration of public buildings. Take the example of a building occupied mainly by the Post Office Department, with the offices of four or five other branches of the federal government located in the same building. Who is responsible for the administration of that building? Suppose there is a parking lot available, who should have the right to say that certain cars shall be parked there and certain cars shall not be allowed to park there, and so on? This is a problem that has created a little fuss and furore on one or two occasions, because apparently there is not a clear line of responsibility. At times the janitor in charge of a building has fought with another official of the Department of Public Works who claimed he had the first right to park his car in a specific area and the postmaster had to take his car around to the back door. I feel that individuals in charge of buildings should be informed as to who is responsible, on the spot, for the administration of these buildings and the decisions as to what preferences exist for the parking of cars and so on.
In regard to designing policy, I should like to know whether certain architects are studying this question, and whether at any time there is consultation with the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada as to a policy respecting the design of public buildings. I should also like to know whether any competitions are being held or are anticipated regarding suitable designs for public buildings.
I have one or two other matters to mention, following which I shall have practically completed my few remarks on the administration item. Last year I made a plea for

the rehabilitation of lover's lane between the back of parliament hill and the Ottawa river; not that 1 have any particular interest in or use for this area, but as it is now it is a very unsatisfactory view for anyone travelling along the Ottawa river by boat.
At the time I mentioned this situation last year the minister stated that he would give the question consideration, and I should like him now to tell this committee what consideration has been given to clearing up this rather unsightly area in order to make it available for people who wish to legitimately enjoy it. I am of the opinion that this project would not cost a great deal of money, although there are certain walks and rails which would have to be repaired and put back into proper condition, and I cannot understand why there is so much hesitation in improving the area.
I have another query with respect to what I am pleased to term "operation statues and lemon juice". I brought this matter to the attention of the minister last year, after the department started a program of rubbing the statues, beginning with that of D'Arcy McGee, with lemon juice, I believe. In this regard I should like to read an article which appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail of June 3, 1960. When I raised this question in the committee last year I received a report that this most unusual operation was proceeding satisfactorily. I later received a letter to the same effect. The article to which I have made reference reads as follows:
Ottawa, June 2-Satisfied with the scrubbing job on D'Arcy McGee and the fair maiden they call Mollie, senior officials of the Department of Public Works have given permission to clean up the remaining eight bronze statues on parliament hill.
The father of confederation, standing on a concrete pedestal, with the buxom Mollie draped at his feet, was recently given a test bath. McGee was chosen because he is at the rear of the centre block, hidden from most of the tourists. Had the test failed it would not have been noticed as readily as the others.
A scrubbing crew removed years of grime from the statue and then rubbed McGee and Mollie with lemon oil.

Mr. Chairman, this is the first time I have spoken in committee since your appointment, and I should like to take advantage, at the outset, of the opportunity to congratulate you in respect to this very high appointment. I do so as one Manitoban to another.
I have a very few brief remarks to make to the minister and his officials this morning, and I hope he will forgive me if I become a a little parochial, inasmuch as I may not be here later on in the day, in making suggestions regarding two or three matters of importance at the present time to the people of the city of Winnipeg.
I believe the minister is aware of the fact that at the present time the Red and Assini-boine rivers which flow through the city of Winnipeg are at very low and dangerous levels, and that the water pollution at the present time in the city of Winnipeg has become very dangerous. There is no effective treatment unit to remove the sewage from these two rivers, and because of the low rate of flow there is a very great possibility of the spread of bacteria followed perhaps, by sickness.
There has been some discussion about the locks at Lockport lower down the river, which were used some months ago and perhaps are still being used to increase the rate of flow so as to raise the level of the water in the rivers at the city of Winnipeg. If at all possible I should like some information from the minister or his officials in this regard.
In addition to that suggestion, but having regard to the sewage treatment unit, I understand that at the present time the city of Winnipeg and the metropolitan council of greater Winnipeg are making application to the minister and his department in relation to the financing of these units, by virtue of the amendment made last fall, under the

Supply-Public Works National Housing Act. When these applications are received I should like them to be given high priority and consideration so that these facilities may be installed at the earliest possible opportunity.
The next subject I wish to refer to, which is of great interest to our senior citizens of the city of Winnipeg, has regard to the expansion of housing facilities for our elderly people. I am sure the minister is aware of the great work done in Winnipeg by the age and opportunity bureau, and will remember receiving a brief from that association with respect to an amendment to the National Housing Act to increase the provision of housing facilities for our senior citizens through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
This organization has made a comprehensive survey of the existing needs of our elderly citizens for increased housing facilities in the city of Winnipeg. Perhaps I may just take a moment or two to place on the record two or three points made manifest by the study carried out by this excellent organization. First of all it discovered that old age assistance and old age pensions are the main source of income of a large percentage of aged persons. They found that those who need accommodation most cannot afford to pay the rent being charged aged persons in limited dividend housing projects provided under existing legislation. They found that the existing regulation for the accommodation of single aged persons is not realistic in that it is impossible to provide the required standards of accommodation at rents compatible with their incomes. They also found that single aged persons constitute a majority of the population over 70 years of age, and that single aged persons cannot live in those units.
I am not going to deal with this matter at great length. The minister has full knowledge of my views and my interest in the matter, and the fact that something should be done with regard to amending or expanding section 16 of the National Housing Act to provide for some type of accommodation which would cover those people. The accommodation would be the hostel type which at the present time is not included under the National Housing Act.
This is not a situation which is signally evident only in the city of Winnipeg. From the information I have I would say that it exists in the larger cities right across Canada. I wonder whether perhaps for a start the minister might take into consideration the appointment of someone-not necessarily from C.M.H.C.; perhaps someone from the Canadian welfare council-to make a study in the


larger cities across Canada to see if the National Housing Act is providing adequate housing facilities for our senior citizens, and whether the hostel type of accommodation is the solution to the problem, if those facilities are not adequate at the present time. I believe most of this information is available now. On the basis of the report on such a survey I think it would become only too apparent that the need is not being fulfilled and something should be done about it. Perhaps the time has come, Mr. Chairman, to give consideration to applying one section of the National Housing Act, or indeed introducing a special act, to housing for aged and senior citizens. This might cover people over 60, 65 or 70 years of age.
I will not dwell any longer on this subject, inasmuch as the brief and the views of the aged and opportunity bureau and myself have been distributed among hon. members. The minister was kind enough to receive the brief, sit down with me and other interested members and explain to us the present provisions of the act and the fact that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation itself, the government and his officials are always interested in looking into things of this sort. I hope he takes heed of what I have said today and perhaps takes a longer look at it.
I might move on to my third and last point, which has to do with slum clearance and urban redevelopment in the city of Winnipeg. Hon. members know that a few days ago I had the special privilege of looking at the Mulberry housing project in the city of Halifax. I was happy to have the opportunity to go down and see it. When I saw it I was astounded to realize that in the city of Winnipeg we probably have some of the worst housing conditions to be found in any of the major cities across Canada. Yet for the last three and a half or four years the city council of Winnipeg has done nothing approaching the Mulberry project in the city of Halifax. The Mulberry project contains 348 units and I am told it will house around 1,500 persons. A project of this kind could be used in the city of Winnipeg at the earliest possible moment.
I am told by the minister and by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation that they are ready, willing and only too eager to get going on the same sort of project for the people in those areas in the city of Winnipeg where more adequate housing and redevelopment are needed. I am sure such a project would bring new business and provide greater economic opportunity for the depressed slum areas. I trust the offer still stands. I should

like to receive the assurance from the minister that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and his officials are interested in this problem. Perhaps he could bring us up to date on just what progress is being made in the city of Winnipeg in regard to this matter.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks this afternoon on one of the divisions of the department which comes under the jurisdiction of the minister. I hope to be as objective as possible. I wonder whether you would call it one o'clock.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps my first words should be words of congratulation to you, sir, on your recent appointment, one that I feel is very well deserved and which I am sure you welcome as another opportunity for service.
In order to appreciate fully the situation in which the housebuilding industry and the government find themselves today, I believe it will be very helpful to review very briefly government activity in this field in the past year. It will be recalled that during almost the first half of 1960 housebuilding had virtually collapsed as the result of government policy. The annually adjusted rate at that time, I believe, averaged something in the order of 60,000.
First there was the reluctance of the government approved lenders to put their money into long term mortgages when more attractive terms and rates were available elsewhere. It will be recalled that the banks stopped lending. The fact that more attractive interest rates and better investment opportunities were available caused the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance to say that these institutions were abdicating their social responsibilities. Yet it was the government's monetary and fiscal policies that had resulted in these higher interest rates throughout the economy.
Further, it will be remembered that during this very period when the approved lenders drastically reduced their lending on housing and the banks refused to lend, the government decided to cut in half the amount it had made available for direct lending during the previous year. Despite the fact that the then minister of trade and commerce had indicated that there would be 140,000 starts in 1960, and the Minister of Public Works at that time forecast 125,000, the government announced
Supply-Public Works
its intention to reduce from $330 million odd to $175 million the money it would make available for direct lending in 1960.
It was hoped-and they had the benefit of good advice, of course-that construction in other fields would take up the slack, but the fact of the matter is that it did not. Therefore at a time when mortgage money could scarcely be found from normal sources, the government sliced in half its lending activity. Little wonder that we ended up the year with 108,000-odd starts. Little wonder that this year, when housebuilding is showing some signs of recovery toward a volume that we might normally expect, the minister is able to stand up and announce increases over last year's depressed figures. But these announcements by the minister only tell part of the story. Despite the minister's fine words, and despite the artificial stimulation that has been given to housing by government legislation, starts have been actually declining since February. I have here the latest figures that are available to me, the dominion bureau of statistics figures for June 7. These are the seasonally adjusted rates: February, 119,000; March, 110,000; April, 90,000.
Hon. members will also realize that more than a shortage of mortgage funds developed in the housebuilding industry last year. During the last half of the year there was a great shortage of buyers which resulted from the overexpansion and overstimulation of the housebuilding industry by the government during 1958 and 1959. Further, I believe that during 1960 and again this year there was and is a growing awareness on the part of the buyers of the tremendous burden of high interest payments at today's 6| per cent rate, which we all know is the highest interest rate in the history of the National Housing Act.
Certainly the government cannot blame the governor of the Bank of Canada for this rate, which was set by the government itself. It is little wonder, then, that the government was desperate last fall in an attempt to find ways and means to get the housebuilding industry back on the rails. It is little wonder that they found it necessary to introduce amendments to existing legislation during the last quarter of the year, and particularly the changes in December.
May I say at once, as I said at the time the legislation was before us in the house, although it was a year too late, to the extent that it increased housebuilding it was welcome. We also recall the imposition of the ceiling on wages. Finally the government raised the ceiling on wages, and then removed it. However, I am not going to go into all these things now.
6382	HOUSE OF
Supply-Public Works I have referred to these activities of the government during the past year or more in order to point out the power of the federal government in this field. The results of the past 17 months have clearly shown the degree of control over housing that can be exercised by any federal government. Where it would appear that total activity might lag, housebuilding can be stimulated. Where it appears that total activity in the economy is straining our total resources, steps can be taken to curtail housebuilding. The degree to which this stimulation or curtailment might be applied is, of course, highly debatable. The power of our federal government to control the rate of housebuilding comes largely from its control over the N.H.A. mortgage market. It controls the supply of mortgage funds by making N.H.A. mortgage rates attractive or unattractive to private lenders by varying the volume of its own lending.
It has been clearly shown in recent years that the volume of housebuilding responds very quickly to changes in the quantity, availability and of course the terms of N.H.A. mortgage money. Restricting housebuilding in times of prosperity while stimulating housebuilding in times of recession is splendid in theory. The difficulty lies in the policy of attempting to produce total stability by deliberately creating instability in housebuilding. These violent fluctuations are indeed costly to the industry and of course ultimately to the purchaser. When the housebuilding industry is overstimulated, inefficient, inexperienced people are attracted into the industry. They often produce homes that regardless of their price, are expensive.
However, it is not this particular aspect of the high cost of housing that I want to pursue here, Mr. Chairman. As I mentioned earlier, today's main deterrent is not the scarcity of mortgage funds but rather the high cost of mortgage funds. In an earlier debate I dealt in some detail with this 6f per cent N.H.A. rate. Suffice it to say today that a person buying a $15,000 home over a 35 year period will pay $22,476 in interest. If the average age of a purchaser under N.H.A. today is slightly over 35 years, he will pay $37,754 for a $15,000 house, will be collecting his old age security pension and may well have his house fall down before the final payment is made.
I would ask hon. members to compare the interest payments made on a specific amount over a period of time at 6J per cent as compared to 54 per cent. I point out that on a $12,000 mortgage amortized over a 30 year period, there is a difference of $4,056. I point out further that the monthly payment for 

this amount of money and for this particular term at 54 per cent, is $65.85 as against $77.10 at a 6f per cent rate.
I remind hon. members of the F.H.A. rate in the United States, which is 54 per cent. I remind hon. members also that N.H.A. rate was 54 per cent under the Liberal administration in 1954, during a period of mild recession. I appeal to the government again, as I have tried to do for the past year, urging them to reduce at once this 6J per cent N.H.A. rate. What possible justification can there have been during the past year of recession and during a period when three quarters of a million people were unemployed, for maintaining this unnecessarily high N.H.A. interest rate? I hope now that we see signs of a professed change of heart on the part of the government, that there will be early action in this regard.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, the government must be aware of their responsibility in monetary and fiscal matters. Let us just for a moment take a peek at how the young, aggressive administration south of the border tackled this matter immediately after taking office. They had inherited a similarly stagnant situation from the previous administration. I should like to refer very briefly to some quotations. The first is from the New York Times of February 28:
United States acts to cut mortgage rates
The government started a direct and high powered effort today to bring down mortgage interest rates.
The same article continues:
The administration's first move was a package of stimulants through federal housing program channels. The most prominently noted part of that package was a reduction of the permissible maximum for rates on mortgages insured by the federal housing administration-to 5J from 52 per cent.
In the Ottawa Citizen of March 15 we find this:
United States driving to lower interest on mortgages
The Kennedy administration is intensifying its campaign to drive down mortgage interest rates. Home owner's borrowing costs have been edging lower but the decline has been too sluggish to satisfy top officials.
In the New York Times of May 22 we find this:
Mortgage rates are moving down
A new phase of the administration's efforts towards lower mortgage interest rates has started bearing fruit already. Another step is under serious consideration.
The Montreal Star of May 27 has this to say:
Kennedy cuts mortgage rates.
That article covered the announcement by the administration of a reduction from 5 J per cent to 5J per cent in interest rates. Surely

the most important component of the real cost of housing is the cost of money. A reduction of only 1 per cent in the interest rate would have more impact on the annual cost of a house than any conceivable improvement in technology. This government should carry out its debt management policy and its monetary policy in such a way as to create the proper kind of economic climate for capital expenditure and investment in housing.
Mr. Chairman, at this point I should like to say a few words concerning the proposed secondary mortgage market. It will be recalled that for the past three years we on this side of the house have recommended the establishment of an effective secondary mortgage market. I can recall that on at least three occasions. I spelled out in some detail my version of one effective phase of a secondary mortgage market. I referred to an institution that would purchase N.H.A. guaranteed mortgages and use them as collateral against the issuance of certificates in small denominations that would be made available to a new type of investor in housing, the small investor. To the extent that this would attract new investors into the mortgage lending field, it would be effective. However, at no time did I envisage the government unloading long term mortgages at discounts that would have the effect of earning handsome profits for the purchaser at the expense of the taxpayer.
Now, I know the Minister of Public Works will say that this is not the case. It should be noted that in his statement to the house on April 17, this matter was not covered. But in a press release outside the house it apparently was stated, as reported in the press throughout the country, that there would be no loss because the money from the sale of these mortgages would be reinvested at these abnormally high rates. Since that time the minister, in response to questions of mine, has refused to say how much of this money will be reinvested.
There is the picture. After a favourable press release, we have silence on this point. I am watching with considerable interest, therefore, the action of the government in this offering of a $15 million nibble which is currently being made. It will be interesting to note the price at which they will be prepared to pass on to the purchasers these $750 million worth of mortgages-

I should like to deal with a matter that is occupying the attention of many of the leaders of the housebuilding industry, namely finding some satisfactory means of facilitating the financing of the older type homes. Surely it cannot be argued that everyone buying a home wants a new house in a new subdivision far removed from his place of work or daily activity. It is becoming daily more and more apparent that this ever spreading development into new raw land is creating tremendous costs in respect of services required and in respect of transportation, etc. However, this has been the trend since the war, and understandably so. The N.H.A. was designed primarily to assist in the construction of new homes, to take care of the tremendous backlog that existed as the result of little or no construction during the war years and indeed during a great part of the thirties.
Today the situation is entirely different. For the first time in 15 years we have seen evidence during the past year that the effective demand has been met. I am not for a moment suggesting that the facilities of the National Housing Act should be diverted from the encouragement of new construction. However, I am fully convinced that the facilities of N.H.A. should be expanded to the extent that the C.M.H.C. could assist in the financing of older type homes along the same lines as is now being done with regard to new construction.
In nearly every Canadian town and city we find older people who have raised their families and who are now living alone in homes much too large for their physical and financial capabilities. Yet these people are forced to live on in these larger homes because no convenient way has been developed to finance the sale of such houses with a small down payment, as is the case with new homes. Therefore the older folks stay on and the younger prospective purchasers are compelled to forgo the opportunity of buying larger homes which might be more in keeping with their family requirements, or resort to some loan shark who will extract the last pound of flesh through a second mortgage. In countless cases families could purchase and properly assume financial responsibility for a moderately priced home but, goodness knows, there are plenty of statistics to prove that
Supply-Public Works
many find the burden of the newer and more expensive homes too great for their incomes. I think the housing statistics put out by the dominion bureau of statistics provide ample proof that 92 per cent of all N.H.A. buyers are earning more than $4,000 a year, so we have reached the point where the National Housing Act in this respect is practically useless to those in the lower income group.
1	believe that making loans available on existing houses would result in a substantial increase in the number of Canadian families owning their homes and this, as I am sure hon. members will agree, would be a highly desirable situation.
As I mentioned earlier, not all families want to live in a particular area that is being developed at the time they are buying a home. It is therefore understandable that under the system I propose, prospective purchasers could buy homes in the locality they prefer.
I think it is apparent to all that if the sales of older homes were encouraged, it would result in an increased demand for new homes. This conclusion is based on the assumption- a proper one, I believe-that the number of potential buyers for older homes would be greatly increased and as a result present owners could sell more easily, cash in their equity and have it available for the purchase of a new home. I therefore urge the government to amend the National Housing Act so as to enable C.M.H.C. to make loans in respect of existing homes along the same lines as loans are presently being made available in respect of new housing. Let us put an end to this discrimination against the owner of an existing house.
Now I should like to turn from something new to an old complaint involving the government's stubborn insistence in clinging to a
2	per cent insurance premium to insure its own mortgages. This is as unrealistic as it is unnecessary, and the record proves it. I will not go as far as some and say that the premium should be eliminated, but most certainly the rate should be reduced. The government's insistence on maintaining the present premium rate adds several hundred dollars to the cost of every home purchased in Canada, not only to the original purchase price but in the financing.
The fund resulting from this premium now stands, I believe, at some $70 million. I believe this fund should be used to assist in making low cost housing available to some of our elderly citizens. The need in this field is great, and with the increase in life expectancy now being experienced the problem will increase. However, I hope to have more to say on this subject at another stage in the examination of these estimates.

I should like to make a further new proposal to the government, namely that home owners who are unemployed for six months or more and who are threatened with foreclosure and the loss of their homes and equities be given special consideration. I propose that a moratorium of 12 months on payments be guaranteed by the government under N.H.A. to home owners who are out of work for a period of more than six months. The slackening of our economic development and the unprecedented level of unemployment demand that attention be given to this problem. The relief I propose should be extended until national prosperity has been restored. This problem is particularly acute in areas where there is long term unemployment. However, losing one's home is a tragedy in any area of this rich young country.
