The hon. member may read what I have said in Hansard. The assistance I have proposed could be given at no cost to the federal treasury, because the borrower at the end of the mortgage term could repay the money which had been advanced on his behalf. Unless something is done in this regard it is my intention at the next session of parliament-and I am assuming there will be another session of this parliament-to introduce a bill incorporating the kind of assistance I have just mentioned. Surely there is something missing in legislation which permits a wage earner who becomes unemployed through no fault of his own to lose his home and, in many cases, a major portion of his savings.
I should like now to say a few words in respect to slum clearance and related matters, and in particular to the financing of renewal projects. I was interested to note that the minister, speaking in Halifax on June 1 to the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities, urged that they speed up the job of weeding out blighted areas within their borders. If I may, I should like to quote the minister, as follows:

Let me say straight away that in my opinion we are not making nearly enough progress in getting rid of slums.
Well, I can tell the minister that we on this side of the house heartily agree with this statement, and have been saying so for some time. In his speech at Halifax the minister went on to reprimand the municipalities for not moving fast enough. As most people know, however, our municipalities would like to move more quickly with regard to these matters, but they are handicapped in their financing by the way the federal government gobbles up the investment dollar at high interest rates. I should like to refer to a publication put out by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities dated May, 1961, and to quote very briefly these words:
The obstacles to municipal borrowing and to the financing of more comprehensive programs of renewal can only be removed by appropriate federal legislation.
The minister might more properly have directed his reprimand to his colleagues who have pursued monetary and fiscal policies leading to higher and higher interest rates. But I do not wish to deal with the shortcomings of the present administration.
The Canadian housing requirements of the future must meet the needs and satisfy the population as a whole rather than any particular segment. At the same time, government must recognize that the earnings of all are not equal. It must also be realized that within each income group there are wide differences or responsibility, due to family numbers, basic managerial ability, incidence of illness and many other relative factors. Any pattern for the future should attempt to provide housing at a price that will afford the greatest opportunity to the greatest number in purchasing their own homes. Such plans must also recognize that there is a large segment of our population which must rent accommodation. Future plans must further recognize the fact that there will also be an increased demand for public housing. This is an economic fact.
In conclusion may I say that we regret the miscalculation and fumbling of the government during most of 1960. We stand ready to commend them, as we have already done, for the worth-while legislation they introduced toward the end of the year. We have for many years urged the establishment of an effective secondary mortgage market which would have the effect of garanteeing a steadier flow of mortgage funds. We think the National Housing Act under both administrations has done an effective job, but believe it should be extended to provide for the financing of older type homes. What was satisfactory in

1954 no longer meets the requirements of 1961. We believe the insurance premium should be reduced. We believe that a moratorium of up to 12 months if necessary be extended to a home owner under N.H.A. who is out of work for six months or more. We believe in a concentrated drive on slum clearance and assistance to municipalities by the establishment of a municipal loan fund, both of which would allow our municipalities to get on with projects badly needed, and which would provide much needed employment in these distressed times.
As I have said on earlier occasions, housing is a most interesting and complex subject and one that will be occupying more and more of our attention and resources as time goes on. Much has been done in the past, but much more remains to be done in the future. When one considers all the social and economic ramifications of this subject in the light of the rapid development in housing which is bound to take place in the foreseeable future, future governments would do well to consider the desirability of a separate department with cabinet status. In this way the housing needs of our people and the economic influences resulting from adequate programming would be assured of a strong voice in government policy, and not just be something tagged on to the end of another department.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I intend to take but a moment, but I know the hon. member for Nipissing would want me to say a word in respect to the National Housing Act interest rate. I should like to tell him again, sir, that this interest rate is based on the yield on long term government bonds and under the N.H.A., as framed by the Liberal government, the yield cannot be more than 2\ per cent above long term government bonds. The present long term yield on government bonds is approximately 5.2 per cent. Therefore the maximum N.H.A. rate, under the rule promulgated by the late Liberal government could be 7J per cent.
However, under our government the present rate is 6f per cent, which is considered to be the lowest competitive rate possible, as compared with other bonds and industrial yields. The decision to adjust the rate twice yearly, which I announced on April 17 last, should keep the N.H.A. rate in relation to other yields. There is no one in Canada who would be more delighted to make it possible to reduce interest rates on N.H.A. loans than myself, as the minister. Having gone through the experience, however, of the approved lenders' funds completely drying up just a few months before I became the minister, when the rate was at 6 per cent, I know what a hazardous expedient it is to reduce
Supply-Public Works
interest rates, as a result of which we can get no money from approved lenders. I am sure my hon. friend, with his knowledge of these matters, and as critic of the opposition in respect to this subject, would not wish the government to exclude private lenders from the market. Otherwise it would cost the federal government hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars per year extra.
In connection with the other suggestion of my hon. friend, that he intends to introduce a bill to declare a moratorium for the benefit of certain people under certain circumstances, might I ask whether he proposes having that measure introduced in each of the provinces or only in the federal parliament? Because it is purely a provincial matter. This is a matter involving property and civil rights, in respect to which the federal government has no authority. Is it his proposition to have someone introduce this measure in the provincial house, or does my hon. friend propose to run for a seat in the legislature of the province of Ontario?
In any event may I say that there are millions of dollars which the approved lenders have invested in N.H.A. mortgages. Is my hon. friend suggesting that the guarantee which has been given to the investor should be done away with, and that a moratorium should be declared so that the mortgage loans which those investors have made in good faith under the terms of the N.H.A., inaugurated originally by the Liberal government and taken advantage of, of course, by the Conservative government, will be seriously affected. Is my hon. friend seriously suggesting there now should be a moratorium in respect of this act?

Mr. Chairman, since the minister has asked me a question I should like to attempt to answer it. First I should like to say that it is surprising how he reconciles his words this afternoon with the criticisms directed toward some of us in this house when the present government was on this side.
In respect to the legislation I proposed, surely it is within the capabilities of a society such as ours to introduce legislation which would have the very humane effect of preventing the wage earner of a family from losing his entire savings as a result of being out of work through no fault of his own.

Mr. Chairman, there are a number of matters of concern to me which are very much related to housing and certain aspects of the housing industry which come under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the estimates for which are contained in vote No. 373. It is not my intention now, during consideration of the first vote of

Supply-Public Works
the Department of Public Works estimates to raise matters which I think should be raised in respect to vote No. 373. However, there is one matter of principle in respect of which I would very much appreciate the comment of the Minister of Public Works.
I should like to ask the minister whether, in his position as minister and under his oath of office, he could give information to this house relating to the letting of contracts under his jurisdiction. I believe I am correct in saying that on tenders being called, they shall be opened on a national basis, that no tender is opened until after a certain deadline, and that those who have tendered have a right to be present at that time.
If I am accurate in suggesting that the tenders must be opened on a national basis, I suggest it would be rather difficult for many individuals who have tendered to be present when they are opened. I should like the minister to inform this committee whether some tenders are opened on a provincial basis and, if so, whether the minister approves. There is a general understanding among subcontractors across Canada that this government, with all its sanctimonious utterances, has a selected list of subcontractors in various fields. Is the minister prepared to stand up before this committee of the whole and state that there is no such selected list at his divisional headquarters?
As my second question I should like to ask on what basis contracts are let by his department at a provincial or divisional level. I know something of the construction industry and I travel in this country a good deal, as a result of which I have come to certain conclusions regarding the letting of contracts. I do not think it will be too much of a shock to the minister when I suggest that the subcontractors of this country are convinced that there is some dirty work going on in the Department of Public Works in respect to the letting of subcontracts.
According to my information subcontracts are handled in a different way from contracts on a national basis in so far as opening the bids is concerned. National bids are not opened until the deadline is reached and those who tender are present. I am informed that in more than one province the situation with respect to subcontracts is most peculiar. Certain people who tender never put in their tender until a few minutes before the deadline. Some of them know what the other tenders were and their tender, put in in the last few minutes, is always just a few dollars lower than the other tenders. I have heard this said in more than one province of Canada. Subcontractors want to know just what is going on.

If my information is correct, and I think it is, I say to the minister that no contract on the national level should be opened until the deadline is reached, and anyone who tenders can be there. What is the policy on contracts let outside of national headquarters of the Department of Public Works? Is it not possible to have a policy in the provinces or at divisional headquarters which would not only remove the suspicion in the public mind and in the contractors' minds that there is the selected list which I mentioned previously, but also remove the definite suspicion and understanding that before the deadline is reached certain contractors know the amount of the tenders of the other subcontractors, and in the last half hour or last few minutes put in their tenders just below the lowest of those that have already tendered?
Through you, Mr. Chairman, I say to the minister there were grave misgivings in many quarters with respect to this matter. I would like the minister to explain the situation in his department with respect to subcontracts and tenders. If the situation is as I am told it is, then there is a lot of dirty work going on and people are getting contracts at the last minute by underbidding because somehow they get previous information. If this situation exists, then this loophole should be plugged so the system of tendering would be put on a honest basis and contracts would be granted honestly.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the situation in connection with tendering in the Department of Public Works is well known and recognized across Canada. Let me start in Ottawa, or on the general level. If there is a contract with an estimated amount of $15,000 or more a universal tender is called. That goes out together with the specifications, and anybody across Canada in entitled to tender. If the project is to be undertaken in a certain area the people in that area naturally would like to see the tender go to a local contractor in that particular area. This is what we would like to do and we get criticism, of course, if it is not done. But we have found that we can save the people of Canada a great deal of money by having the tender open for everybody to bid on.
For the information of my hon. friend who has just made a statement without any supporting facts, and who is simply asking questions, which he is entitled to do, may I say that when the tender is called the date is set out and the hour up to which a tender or bid can be made. At that hour the tenders are closed. After that hour bids which come in, even a couple of minutes after the hour, are too late. The tenders or bids are then

opened by a department official, or two department officials, sometimes three, and in the presence of a representative of the Canadian Construction Association.
I wish to pay my tribute to the Canadian Construction Association for the tremendous assistance they have been to me during my two-year period as Minister of Public Works, for the suggestions they have made and for the advice I have able to get from them from time to time when I have asked for it on certain tenders. We have found it a wonderful thing. We also have present the people who have bid on the project. Until the bids are opened they are under seal. They are all opened together and there can be no complaint, lest anybody should suspect that favouritism is shown, because they see them all opened. Each of the bidders can be there with the representative of the Canadian Construction Association.
My hon. friend referred to subcontracts. May I tell him that when a bid is made in response to a universal tender the applicant has to set out the subcontractors specifically, and he is not entitled to change those. He has to go ahead with them and use them if he is awarded the contract. In the old days it used to be possible to set out certain subcontractors when the tender was put in and then change them later on. That has all been done away with. We feel we have a fool-proof and, let me say, an honest system.
In connection with local tender calls for small undertakings, there are day labour jobs, as the hon. member for Vancouver East knows. We do not undertake these projects if it is at all possible to avoid them because sometimes they are quite costly. On smaller undertakings in a local area we call for local bids, where anybody can and is invited to bid. The undertaking is advertised in the local newspaper and in the local post office, and the lowest of the bids is accepted. On very small undertakings, such as supplying material or doing a small job, we have what are called invited tenders, where the official engineer in charge of the local office in the area can decide who in that area could supply, shall we say, a stove or some other material.
Does he have a list in front of him?

speechtext: No list from our department, no. Under no circumstances has he a list.
Will you stand there and say there is no selected list?

Yes, I do.

I have stated that there is no list. Is my hon. friend suggesting that the Department of Public Works would send out lists to our local engineers all over Canada containing names of those whom they should ask to bid on these local projects? The low bidder among the invited tenderers in the local area gets the contract, whatever it happens to be. We have found this practice eminently successful.
I know that I am bitterly criticized time and time again, week in and week out, for being so strict. If there is anything of which I am perhaps guilty it is the fact that I have been as strict as I have in my two years as minister. I know that many of the backbenchers on my side of the house feel that I am unnecessarily strict.
They seem to enjoy it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
However, those are the rules in the Department of Public Works. We have tried to work out rules and if at times I appear to be too strict it is because I am endeavouring to follow the rules.
As far as any complaints are concerned, it will be recalled that last year the hon. member for Villeneuve referred to a situation involving day labour work, and as the hon. member for Vancouver East knows this is sometimes difficult to deal with. Away off in the hinterlands you will have a foreman running a job and hiring help. The hon. member will realize how difficult it is to supervise these matters even though they involve small projects. The result is that trouble can arise. In that instance we not only investigated but we prosecuted and put certain people in jail. Some of them are still in jail.
I should like to make a suggestion to the hon. member who has been a member of the house for many years and who, when he led the C.C.F. party in the province of British Columbia, was within one seat of being the premier of that province. I know he will not put a bogus case before me because there is nothing bogus about the hon. member. I would ask him to give me any information he has about any situation which he himself has investigated, not just the wild statements of people who have missed out because they did not make the low bid or because, as I pointed to the hon. member for Hull last year, they were incompetent to carry out the contract, or because they were financially incapable of doing so. If the hon. member has any instance where the government has not followed the rules on which I have elaborated at some length because of the respect I have for the hon. member, I would ask him to let the department know and we will investigate the matter and, if necessary, we will prosecute.

Supply-Public Works
If there is any misconduct on the part of our officials, we will fire them, and every official of the department across Canada knows that. General Young, my deputy, summons the engineers to Ottawa every year and we go into these matters carefully and fully, Every official knows where we stand on this subject. If the hon. member does not mind me saying so, he will appreciate that unless we have specific examples to verify, support or bolster statements made it is very hard for us to do anything except to outline the general situation. I invite the hon. member and all other hon. members at any time and under any circumstances to bring to my attention any variation from these rules. The department is, of course, a vast one. We are spending more than twice as much as the Liberals did in an effort to solve unemployment and develop the country.
With less consequence.
He is reading aloud.

speechtext: I wish the hon. member for Essex East would note that I have not had any notes for this particular discourse. I say to hon. members that they should bring these things to our attention. It will be appreciated that there may be some derelictions as we found in a certain township away off in the hinterlands last year in connection with a day labour contract. Bring these matters to our attention and we will investigate them. In the Department of Public Works we feel that by following this system we are saving the taxpayers of Canada millions of dollars every year.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to pose a question to the minister on this subject. The Depuiy Chairman: Order. I think it would be fairer to the members of the committee if they would follow the rotation
(Mr. Walker.]

which is listed before me here in the order that they have presented their names to me. Mr. Chairman, since over half of British Columbia's 15,000 miles of coast line lies within the constituency of Comox-Alberni, I feel called upon to make a few remarks on this item. In the constituency of Comox-Alberni in particular there is a multitude of scattered communities without, in many cases, interconnection by roads. This results in the Department of Public Works being called upon to spend huge sums of money for wharves, floats, boat harbours and other such maritime services.
The residents of the communities to which I have referred are undoubtedly more interested in the work of this department than in that of any other department of the government. Because of rapid development, particularly in the northern part of Vancouver island and along the west coast of that island, and because of the ever-changing pattern of transportation, demands for expenditures are heavy and will be increasingly so. Where wharves and floats were not required a few years ago, in some cases there is now an urgent necessity, and the need for safe mooring facilities for the large fishing fleets we have on the coast and the small coastwise merchant ships such as tugs and small freighters is a need that must be met as soon as possible in many areas.
I have already brought to the attention of the minister and his officials the need for public docks in several places. One is Tahsis and another one is Gold river on the west coast of Vancouver island. I have pointed out the need for safe harbour facilities between the Ballenas islands and Campbell river. This is the course that ships follow as they go up the coast of British Columbia. It is an area in which it is extremely difficult to find a safe anchorage during a severe storm. In the past there have been a number of lives lost in that area, some within the past year, and I feel that both lives and shipping could be saved if a safe anchorage were provided at an appropriate spot. I know the department is giving consideration to the essential requirements of Kelsey bay. This is the present terminus of the island highway and because of the number of boats that require moorage in that area I urge the minister to proceed with this project at the earliest possible date.

The residents of Parksville-Qualicum beach area, as well as those on Lasqueti island, are grateful for the item included in these estimates for the reconstruction of the French Creek boat harbour. This project should be expedited as the present facilities are daily becoming less usable by the commercial fishing fleet and other boats.
The requirements I have mentioned lately are but a few of the essential ones along that part of the coast. The people of the area are quite aware of, and greatly appreciate, the large sums of money that have been spent on public works in the last three years. I know that the total amounts to several millions of dollars, and I also know that a trip along the coast line of the Comox-Alberni constituency-which I hope the minister will have an opportunity to make this summer- will convince the minister that millions more are needed to fill the essential needs.
As I said before, development in some areas is at a rapid pace. New pulpmills are contemplated in the near future, and there has been a tremendous development in mining in this area which, until recently, was not considered by some government departments to have much promise. All of these developments require extended wharf facilities and other public works. New mines are coming into production, resulting in new communities, and development programs involving many millions are under way. I am sure the department will do its best to provide the works, such as wharves, boat harbours and floats, that come under their jurisdiction.
I should like to speak for a moment on a subject which I have raised before, namely, the question of the trans-Canada highway on Vancouver island. I know the minister gave a short, and perhaps one might say a rather sharp, answer to the Hon. Mr. Gaglardi, minister of highways for British Columbia, to his telegraphed request for extension of the trans-Canada highway to the north end of the island. The manner in which the request was made no doubt gave rise to the answer which was sent. However, I do believe the people of Vancouver island are entitled to have the minister give serious consideration to this proposal. The mistake of designating only 70 miles of the highway on an island over 300 miles long as part of the trans-Canada route, is one for which the government of British Columbia must accept the greater part of the blame.
The minister has said on several occasions that his first interest is in the completion of the first trans-Canada highway. I am not talking about a part of a second trans-Canada highway, I am talking about an extension of the present one to its rightful terminal, the most westerly accessible point 90205-6

403J
Supply-Public Works
on the Pacific coast. While I am referring to the extension of this highway, I might say that the British Columbia government recently received, or expects to receive, from this government, a subsidy for the construction of its two proposed ferries operating between the mainland and Victoria. I believe this will probably amount to something over $2 million. I think it would be only fair for the provincial government to use this $2 million for the development of a highway in the northern part of Vancouver island.
I spoke earlier, Mr. Chairman, about changing patterns of transportation along the Pacific coast. Many communities formerly served by coastal vessels sailing from Vancouver are now served by ferries from Vancouver island points. In the past the federal government assumed full responsibility for the construction of the necessary steamer docking facilities at these communities. In some cases these so-called steamer docking facilities are no longer required because the communities are served by ferries from Vancouver island. I feel it is only fair that the federal government should accept responsibility for these necessary ferry landings. As I said before, the traditional type of wharf is no longer required. The government had no hesitation in the past in accepting responsibility for the old type steamer wharf, so I think they should give some consideration to accepting some responsibility for these necessary ferry landings.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like to express my appreciation, and I think I speak for my constituents, of the consideration that the minister and his officials have given to the multitude of requests that come from a constituency such as mine. I should like to say that I warn the minister, in case he is about to mention Ripple rock and all the money that was spent there a number of years ago, if he brings up that subject, I am going to agitate amongst the diehards in Victoria that we start a campaign to have the hole filled up again and this will cost a lot more money than the cost of blowing up the rock.

I have a few matters concerning my constituency which require the attention of the department, the estimates of which are now before us. Some time ago I received a letter containing a resolution passed by the corporation of the city of Fort William which reads as follows, and I quote:
That whereas it has been very evident that municipalities have very great difficulty due to the increased use of automobiles and heavy trucking through and over city streets in trying to maintain and keep up with the increasing demand for roads and also the increased standards required for present day heavy vehicular traffic. The cost therefore, has risen beyond the ability of the

Supply-Public Works
municipalities to adequately cope with it. This problem has been recognized in part by the federal government in the United States and they are increasing their assistance to the municipalities for road construction.
Therefore be it resolved that we request the federal government to make realistic appraisal of the plight of the municipalities in respect to road construction with the view of setting up the policy to participate with the municipality and the province in sharing the costs of all road construction within the municipalities.
I realize, Mr. Chairman, that it has not been federal policy to assist financially in road construction within municipalities. However, it seems to me that the time may be opportune to give such a policy some serious consideration. It could be set out in a formula similar to the winter works incentive program which would create job opportunities for many unemployed. I urge the minister to keep such a proposal in mind which, if adopted, would receive the commendation of every municipality in Canada.
Last year, again at the request of the Fort William city council, I brought to the attention of the minister the need for breakwater protection for the McKellar and Mission islands facing lake Superior within the city of Fort William. These two islands which form part of the harbour frontage of the city are exposed to the lake and require the protection of a breakwater, from the present breakwater which protects a portion of the mainland fronting on Port Arthur. At the present time the Canadian Pacific Railway own a large area of land on McKellar island which would be ideal for industrial use if it had breakwater protection, and the same statement applies to a large tract of property located on the Mission island.
Another major obstacle which is retarding the full use of these two islands and which must be removed is that at the present time there is only one bridge connecting the mainland with the Mission island and a second bridge connecting the Mission island with the McKellar island. In the event that anything happens to the bridge connecting the mainland, it will have the effect of separating both islands completely from the mainland. It will therefore be seen that another bridge between the mainland and the Mission island is absolutely essential.
The building of another bridge would remove the main objection against the almost immediate development of these islands for potential industrial expansion, which includes the probability of a steel mill since Premium Ore Company which is headed by Cyrus Eaton, the chairman of the board of Steep Rock Iron Mines, has an option on the Mission island for such a project.
In an article written for the industrial edition of the Fort William Daily Times

Journal, Senater N. M. Paterson, a man of great experience and vision made the following statement:
The seaway will gradually develop as it takes time to change methods and deepen channels which will be required over the next few years, but I would like to take this opportunity to point out the necessity of building a new bridge from the island across the Mission river to the mainland so that if anything happened to the railway bridge in Westfort there would be an alternative route rather than Slate river.
It would be a most serious thing to all the traffic which crosses that bridge daily if the wind happened to catch a ship going through the bridge and twisted the bridge from its foundation. We must attract the authorities' attention to this important matter as with foreign ships going in, anything is liable to happen.
Those living at the head of the lakes do not see the development as one who goes there periodically and to me the progress is as amazing as we see in eastern cities in proportion.
I do not think I need to add more to the senator's statement which emphasizes the very real danger that some day something might happen to the present lone bridge, except to say that the new bridge would also serve as a highway to further development of harbour facilities, and it is generally conceded that when expansion in the seaway dock now under construction becomes necessary, the only desirable area available will be on these two islands.
My constituents are very grateful to the government for the lakehead seaway terminal now under construction, which will be a great asset not only to the lakehead area but to the prairie provinces, as intimated by their respective premiers on numerous occasions, because it will improve the transshipping of goods and materials east and west and vice versa.
Another matter of considerable importance to the area with which the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Labour are particularly familiar is the need1 for a new public building to replace the old dilapidated 70-year old structure which houses the national employment office. The building in question was the post office vacated some 30 years ago. It is a fire trap and it is totally inadequate for the services for which it is put into use.
The department has an ideal site with a frontage of 273 feet by 140 feet centrally located with ample parking facilities. It is no secret that the Minister of Labour has recommended that the construction of a new building be given earliest consideration. The anticipation was that in the estimates of 1960-61 provision would be made for this project. I regret very much to find that the decision to build has again been postponed.
During the Easter recess I paid a visit to the national employment office and, as I

expected, I found the place crowded with people in every nook and corner. Office workers and job seekers could hardly be distinguished. The corridors were cluttered and when I asked one of the officials if they had toilet facilities for visitors, the answer I received was that washroom facilities available were limited for the staff on the third floor of the building-which by the way has no elevator; you have to walk up-and inadequate even for the office workers.
One of the officials from the Winnipeg office, namely Mr. L. T. Fraser, after an inspection, recently made a report to the effect that inasmuch as it will take two or more years before the new building is erected, he would recommend that between 1,000 to 1,200 square feet of suitable office space be leased as close as possible to the present premises which he considers insufficient for the claims pay function, but which would provide accommodation for the male placement division.
This is clearly a situation which should not be allowed to worsen before taking action and, if the government is trying to alleviate unemployment by such means, among others, and if a stimulation is needed in public works, what is the government waiting for? I doubt whether there is a national employment office the facilities of which are as poor and inadequate as those at the Fort William office which serves an area of 70,000 people. There are other departments of the federal government which are paying rent in the city of Fort William and I cannot see why there should be any delay in providing a building which would house other services as well.
The annual report of proceedings under the Trans-Canada Highway Act for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1960, contains a statement that the trans-Canada highway project provided 1,531,155 man days-eight hours-of employment during the one year; and labour created by the supply of materials and services estimated at an additional 2,602,964 man days of eight hours.
From this statement it can be seen that road work absorbs a substantial number of our labour force and what is even more important, it provides jobs for the most part to the unskilled labour.
In the absence of any other similar projects which would employ a large number of people, I submit that the government should give serious consideration to the construction of a four-lane national highway.
Plans for a six-lane expressway to serve Malton airport from Toronto are completed. It will replace the old two-lane highway which has been a bottleneck responsible for
Supply-Public Works
many delays and accidents. I only wish I could now offer congratulations to those responsible for the planned improvement, on similar action in connection with the highway west of the lakehead.
During the debate on the trans-Canada highway resolution last year, I drew attention to the poor condition of the highway west from Fort William to the Manitoba boundary. Complaints had been pouring in from various organizations and travellers. Now, a year later, with the exception of a few stretches, the highway resembles a trail of potholes. I realize that the upkeep of the trans-Canada highway is not the responsibility of the minister. Should it not then be the responsibility of the federal government to ascertain that before any contribution is made there should be some assurance that a fair standard for the highway is established for every part of the country. Speaking of road conditions in the province of Ontario, what we need is a national co-ordinated system which would serve the national interest in case of an emergency. Existing traffic arteries leading out of our major cities, including our capital city, do not have the capacity to evacuate the population, should that become necessary.
It is because of these considerations among others, not the least of which are the safety and convenience of the people, that a conference should in my view be convened by the government to consider these matters together with the provinces and major municipalities, traffic engineers and the good roads association.
The Canadian tax foundation in its study of taxes and traffic has this to say on the subject, and I quote:
Undoubtedly, highways have some "national" implications in Canada, just as they have provincial and municipal implications, and these are probably broader than the federal government has been willing to recognize in the past. The Trans-Canada Highway Act and some of the earlier legislation has been in the right direction and more of this type of program should be planned for the future.
The "national" implications of highways in Canada are far more intangible than in most other countries-particularly in the United States-and the danger is that they will be valued too low rather than the reverse. We shall not truly be a national community until it is possible for the masses of our citizens who own cars to travel the country from coast to coast in comfort and safety during at least the milder times of the year.
Just where the line falls between national effort that will achieve this end and federal assistance to the provinces and municipalities in meeting their normal responsibilities for highways, roads and streets cannot be said categorically, but undoubtedly experience and experiment would produce some workable rules. Whenever the line is drawn it should be consistent with the concept of highway financing set out previously.

Supply-Public Works
This statement bears out conclusively the need for a greater and an intensified effort towards the establishment of a national system of highways.
In the interest of safety on our highways I draw attention to the study which was made in the state of Kansas last year which revealed that highway accidents dropped by 25 per cent when white lines or guide lines were painted along the edge of all roads outside urban centres. I should, therefore, like to impress the minister and his officials with the immediate necessity of pressing those responsible to have the edges of highways painted white. I am confident that is a commendable measure which might be the means of saving many lives and preventing many unnecessary accidents.
Now I come to another matter which may appear to be only of minor importance, but I want to assure the minister that in the eyes of hundreds of people who are concerned the subject which I am about to discuss is of considerable interest. It has to do with the accommodation of the income tax office in the city of Fort William which serves the entire area of Thunder Bay including the city of Port Arthur. Several weeks ago I pointed out in a letter to the Minister of National Revenue, the need for the renovation of this building. I am hoping that the Minister of Public Works will have someone in his department look into the conditions which exist in this public building. A month ago I had an opportunity to inspect these premises which were constructed in 1912 and which now serve five times the number of people they were designed to accommodate. The building is shared with the customs office which occupies the lower floor. The receiving area of the income tax office is totally inadequate, space being wasted in one place and cramped in another. I am not asking for a new building. I am being modest. .A good renovation job and the replacement of creaking chairs by more comfortable furniture together with an improvement in seating capacity would be a satisfactory approach.
I could bring other matters to the attention of the minister, however, I wish to be modest in my requests and want only to emphasize the importance of certain things which are essential, namely: early consideration for breakwater protection for the Mc-Kellar and Mission islands in lake Superior; assistance in the building of a new bridge over the Mission river in order to prevent isolation of those two islands where millions of dollars are invested in industry, including an oil refinery, a hydro steam generating station, and several oil storage plants, in the event of a possible break in the present
[Mr. Badanai.j

bridge; the construction of a federal building to house the national employment service and other federal services; restoration of the old customs building and consideration in respect to an improved trans-Canada highway.
I submit these suggestion with the knowledge that implementation of these requests will not only benefit my constituency alone, but will directly and indirectly have a beneficial effect shared by all Canadians.
One further matter to which I wish to refer, and which has caused considerable irritation, is the manner in which announcements are made in respect to government projects affecting members' constituents. As an example of what I refer to, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation a few weeks ago released a number of welcome announcements having to do with items such as the federal loan for the sewage project at Langenburg, Saskatchewan. These announcements were all made by the hon. member for Melville, the member concerned, on behalf of the minister.
Other announcements concerning similar projects at Tugaske and Dinsmore, Saskatchewan were made by the hon. member for Mackenzie as well as the announcement in respect to the project regarding an old people's home, made by the hon. member for St. Boniface.
An announcement was also made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in respect of his own constituency in Vancouver which demonstrates that, notwithstanding the fact that his duties are of an exalted nature, he feels that an elected representative should properly regard any announcement of this nature as being his prerogative.
That pattern is not always followed. For instance, there was announcement made regarding a sewage plant for Willow Bunch, which is in the constituency of Assiniboia, but was the hon. member representing that area notified of that project? Mr. Chairman, that represents everything I wish to bring to the attention of the minister at this stage, and I am sure he will give consideration to my suggestions. I have great faith in the competent officials of his department who have years of experience in this

department. I suggest all they need is a little encouragement from the minister and his approval so they can go ahead and do that job for which they are admirably equipped.

Mr. Chairman, I find myself in rather a peculiar situation because I have made notes which I intended to read. However, because of events which have taken place recently in this committee, I hesitate to do so. I am left with two courses to follow;
I can rip up the notes and write a letter to the minister, or perhaps I can go ahead and speak off the cuff. Unfortunately, for some time I have been living on a basis of tightening up my belt and find myself now with shirts without sleeves, so the cuffs are gone.
I should like to say that it is a great pleasure on my part to take part in this debate on the estimates of the Department of Public Works. This department, under the very capable and industrious minister, has contributed greatly to the improvement of the economy of Canada. I congratulate the minister and the officials of his department for the excellent work that is being done. In spite of the doom and gloom and the pessimistic crepe hanging of certain individuals, the minister has proceeded with courage and faith to build up Canada so that Canadians can enjoy that prosperity which is rightfully theirs. The minister's program of allotting public works funds to all the provinces of Canada and to the localities where they are most needed and will do the most good, has certainly paid off. It is noticeable that he is consistent in this program.
I wish to bring to the attention of the minister the necessity of a breakwater at Chemainus, British Columbia. Chemainus has been a port of export since the first sailing vessel cleared the harbour in 1861. The MacMillan, Bloedel and Powell River Limited mill at Chemainus is the second largest mill in Canada and the sixth largest in the world. Well over 100 deep-sea ships load at this port annually, and in 10 months in 1959, 126 ships loaded and sailed to all parts of the world. Harbour dues paid since January 1954 to December 1959 amounted to $52,991.41, and in 1959 alone amounted to $10,903.14.
The people of that area pay personal income tax on a payroll in excess of $7 million annually and I am sure the government receives a substantial amount from corporation income taxes from the mill in that area. From all sources the federal government has received millions of dollars of revenue from Chemainus over the past years, yet all that has been built there by the federal government is one government wharf, one spar buoy
Supply-Public Works
and one gas flasher light at the harbour entrance. There is not one permanent government structure in Chemainus to show for 99 years of progress and taxes paid. Even the post office and customs office are rental property. The following figures show the investment which has been made in that area up to 1959. MacMillan, Bloedel and Powell River, wharves and structures, $9 million; inventories of logs, lumber and chips in scows, $1,100,000; and scows, $200,000, totalling $10,300,000. There is also a railroad ferry slip in the amount of $50,000; a federal government wharf, $75,000; a provincial government wharf, $90,000; construction by Island Wharves Limited, $30,000; eleven tugs belonging to Chemainus Towing Limited, $125,000; construction by Western Forest Products, $75,000; fishing vessels, $100,000; 138 pleasure boats, $100,000; and a marine taxi, $10,000.
Other investments in Chemainus are a British Columbia power commission thermal plant in the amount of $15 million and other MacMillan and Bloedel buildings making a grand total of well over $40 million.
Moorage for small craft provided in the harbour is as follows: the government wharf, 1,060 feet, Western Forest industries float, 1,500 feet and other floats, 250 feet.
During 1959 over 1,000 small craft used the port of Chemainus to clear customs, to shop for supplies and to take on fuel and ice. This port is open to the north, northwest and west winds which have a sweep of five to 15 miles of open water. Even during July and August the winds have kept small craft from entering the harbour. These two months are the best months of the boating season and the lack of a breakwater has caused a serious loss of business to local merchants as cruisers enter the harbour, note the lack of protection, turn and sail to better anchorage.
The federal government could and should construct a rock-filled breakwater from Hospital point to the spar buoy and Chemainus would then become a safe and secure harbour. The people of Chemainus have tried for years to get this breakwater built and I suggest to the minister that this request be reviewed and work started as soon as possible.
There are certain locations in Canada where a program of public works makes a great difference to the welfare and prosperity of the people living there. One such place is Ganges, on Salt Spring island. There are no large payrolls or industry at Ganges and the establishment of a boat basin would undoubtedly add to the prosperity of that wonderful harbour. I urge the minister to give this matter immediate and careful consideration.
The Department of Public Works has made a survey in connection with a boat basin at

Supply-Public Works Ganges, and I have been advised that the proposal has been placed on the department's advance planning program. Each year hundreds of boats cruise the waters of Salt Spring island; many of them go to Ganges harbour but because of the great popularity of Ganges there is not enough mooring space for them. Ganges harbour lies in the centre of the best cruising waters in the world. Ganges has all the facilities needed to make it the best boating centre on the west coast. They have boat repair yards, a fine hospital, good doctors, stores and shops as required by the boating public.
I ask that the minister give this important matter very serious consideration and that a start be made on a boat basin as soon as possible. It will have to be done sometime and I believe that now is the time to get on with it as the people of Ganges have waited long enough for something that should have been done years ago.

Mr. Chairman, I shall begin my remarks on the estimates of this very important department by expressing my appreciation to the minister and his staff of their many acts of courtesy extended to me from time to time, both in Ottawa and in Newfoundland, and to assure the minister that they have helped me in no small way in passing on important information to my constituents. However, as can be expected, I did not always agree with the minister or with the decision of his officials; but I must thank them for the prompt replies and assure the minister that as long as I am a member from Newfoundland I shall work in the best interests of that province.
This committee is aware but sometimes forgets that Newfoundland entered this great dominion, which now stretches from the Atlantic to the Pacific, as the tenth province only in 1949, and we shall, therefore, be a long time in catching up with even the Atlantic provinces which themselves are by no means the richest provinces.
Canada is not a number of provinces grouped together but a great dominion comprised of 10 provinces united for the common good of its people, and as a province is weak so is the nation. No chain can be stronger than its weakest link. Weakness in one part impairs the whole nation, and if we have one weak province then we cannot have a healthy and prosperous nation.
Newfoundland is an island of approximately 43,000 square miles with a coast line of 6,000 miles. In Newfoundland we have problems which are unique and which do not exist in any other province and therefore should be treated as such.

I am well aware that the Department of Public Works has spent much money in Newfoundland on public works but no more than is spent proportionately in other provinces. For a number of years Newfoundland was completely dependent on its fisheries. While this position has changed somewhat, nevertheless it is a very important industry and ties in with the logging industry.
The department proposes to improve facilities in many communities along the bleak coast of Newfoundland and for this I am grateful, particularly for the proposed construction of the public wharf at Dildo, Trinity bay, where there is a large whaling and fresh fish operation. It is from here that the only mink feed delivery service operates in Canada. This is essential to the existence of 20,000 mink in the 20 ranches in this area.
In addition, this wharf provides shelter for the fishermen to moor their boats and as a result they will be able to fish later in the fall of the year. Every year because of the spring storms and the ice that floats around our coast many repairs have to be made to the public wharves, slipways, stages and so forth. In addition there is always a great need for the dredging of the harbours and coves. I am pleased to learn that the Department of Public Works intends to do some dredging this year in some seven communities in my riding. I believe this work will prove highly beneficial.
I would also urge the minister to see that as much work as possible be done early in the spring so that the fishermen can get the benefit of those services which have been provided and at the same time get badly needed employment.
I am well aware that everything cannot be done in all communities of Newfoundland in any one year, but there are a few places in particular which I should like to mention at this time, even though they have already been brought to the attention of the minister by way of petitions, letters, personal meetings or by telephone calls. I am now thinking of settlements which I know are very important as far as our fisheries are concerned.
First, I call the minister's attention to the need for improving facilities in the Port-deGrave area, including Hibbs Cove, where a breakwater is badly needed. In 1959 I understand that 9 million pounds of fresh fish were produced in that community and when the water is rough the fishermen have to go three miles to discharge their catch and then truck it back to their stages to salt it. The harbour is so crowded with boats that the fishermen can walk across the cove by

stepping from one boat to another. If a breakwater were constructed it would give the fishermen much more space in which to carry on their work.
In the Port de Grave area we have as good fishermen as will be found in any part of Canada. I understand there is a firm which would erect a fresh fish filleting plant in the Port de Grave area if improvements were made to the harbour facilities.
I also request improvements in Harbour Grace, which is one of the most important fishing communities in Newfoundland. Here we have one of the most modern fresh fish processing plants in North America, owned and operated by one of the most progressive firms in the industry, namely North Eastern Fish Industries Limited. This plant is very beneficial not only to the immediate area but also to many persons in Trinity and Conception bays. Last year there were in operation out of Harbour Grace nine boats 36 feet long and over, five boats 32 feet long and over, 12 fishing boats under 32 feet and a number of other small boats. The condition of the public wharf at Harbour Grace is bad and not suitable for the tying up of small fishing boats. There is no place where the fishermen can haul up their boats or moor them in safety. A petition has been forwarded to the minister by the fishermen at Harbour Grace and because of the great necessity of a wharf I again urge the minister to give this matter further consideration. I would also ask him to consider the construction of a haul-out at Harbour Grace similar to the one which the Department of Transport proposes to construct at Clarenville this year.
I would also be grateful if the minister would consider the need for a fishermen's landing at Carbonear. I am pleased to learn that the department proposes to repair the government wharf there this year.
At Chapel Arm and Butter Cove in Trinity bay there are no public wharves and I must again ask the minister to see if his department will construct wharves there.
Again I must ask the minister to give sympathetic consideration to the petitions submitted by the fishermen of Melrose, Trinity bay. One petition was dated February 16, 1960, and another March 6, 1961, and nothing has been done notwithstanding the fact that the majority of the voters supported the friend of the minister. I am aware that many investigations have been made in this harbour and unfavourable reports were received. The fishermen at Melrose do not agree with the results of the investigations of the officials, and they think that improvements could be made to the harbour at a cost much less than the estimates submitted to the minister.

The fishermen of Melrose have never had a public wharf of any kind and have to carry on their avocation in the same manner as their ancestors did 100 years ago. During the national Liberal rally a committee unanimously recommended the construction of a major auditorium in Ottawa for the accommodation of large national gatherings. This resolution was submitted by the Newfoundland delegation and was enthusiastically endorsed by the national problem subcommittee. At the present time it is difficult to hold meetings in the national capital, Ottawa, and the present facilities are such that they discourage large conventions from coming here.
During the Liberal rally many temporary rooms were set up in the agricultural section of the coliseum in which committees could hold meetings. Most of the committees, owing to pressure of work, were meeting at the same time. The rooms were far from soundproof. As a matter of fact, when a speaker with a loud voice was talking in an adjacent room it was sometimes thought we had two speakers in the same room talking at the same time, which reminded us of what takes place sometimes in this house. The rooms were so poorly lighted and so crowded that they reminded us of the black hole of Calcutta. In my opinion it is the duty of the federal government to see that such a building is erected in Ottawa, a city in which every Canadian should take an interest and of which we should all be proud.
I should also like the minister to give consideration to the erection of a public building in Brigus, Conception bay. At Brigus there is a building that is outdated in every respect and is in a bad state of repair. The present building is used by officials of the department of welfare, the forestry division,

Supply-Public Works the post office and for a court house, and is quite often used for public meetings also.
I should like to speak for a few minutes on the trans-Canada highway. The trans-Canada highway, when completed from the western end of Newfoundland to St. John's, the capital, will cover approximately 600 miles, about 200 of which have been paved and about 100 of which are ready for paving. I understand that it will cost about $50 million to construct and pave the remainder of the mileage of the trans-Canada highway. Newfoundland has the second lowest population of all the provinces and the highest road mileage per capita.
The terms of the agreement respecting the proportion of the cost paid by each province should be based on the cost of living in each province and the taxes collected from the people, coupled with the earning power of each province. Newfoundland has a claim to some special consideration with regard to financing because at the present time she is the only province that does not have a standard gauge railway. Newfoundland has a narrow gauge railway and this is a great problem.
Newfoundland and the Atlantic provinces also, I believe, have not as yet enough local roads to provide the means of transportation required to transport provisions from one part of the province to another. This is urgently required for the maintenance of the people and to help the province toward progress and prosperity. It will not be until secondary roads are provided that the Atlantic provinces will even consider the completion of another trunk highway, let alone completion of the trans-Canada highway. At this time, to these provinces of the Atlantic region, especially Newfoundland, the trans-Canada highway seems like something away off in the distance, a beautiful dream. This is the way it will remain unless the federal government come to realize that, if the trans-Canada highway is to be completed within the lifetime of any of us now living, they will have to shoulder their duty and responsibility to all the Canadian people and make the necessary provisions to have this highway completed by providing the required financial assistance. If the federal government intends to continue its present formula, then it is just as well to face the fact that the trans-Canada highway will never be completed. Consequently, the economy of Canada will suffer because of the neglect of those regions which most need and most deserve federal support.

In addition, Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister whether the C.M.H.C. and the national research council have carried out or are still carrying out joint studies to provide Canada with a national building code. estimates of the Minister of Public Works, I do wish to bring to the attention of the minister certain projects which are of particular concern to my constituents in Gloucester. The minister is aware, I am sure, as are his officials, that numerous requests have been received by his department for the development of the port of Bathurst. Last year a delegation from the town of Bathurst met with the minister and his officials and presented a definite request to improve the accommodation at that particular port. I wish the minister could tell us, before he closes the debate on this item, what progress has been made in this direction. I understand that the request was for the dredging of a 23-foot channel in order to accommodate ocean-going vessels.
No later than yesterday a most important announcement was made by the premier of New Brunswick to the effect that Brunswick Mining and Smelting, which has been idle for a number of years, will soon resume operations and so will Consolidated Mining in the same area. The premier of New Brunswick went further and stated that by 1963 a smelter will be erected in that area in order to take care of the production of these mines. If this project is completed, there will be a definite necessity for the development of harbour accommodation and I hope that the co-operation of the federal government will be forthcoming at that time.
I should like to bring to the ministers attention certain requests which have been before the department for some time relating to some of the important fishing communities in my constituency. In Maisonnette, for example, we have about 40 or 45 fishing boats in operation. Fishing is the only industry in that community. Notwithstanding the fact that these fishermen have available a small landing of about 275 feet in length with a depth of water of a foot and a half at low tide, last year they landed over 1.5 million pounds of fish. I understand that the department has had in hand for the last two years a plan for the extension of the present wharf. I understand that this extension could be carried out at an estimated cost of approximately $165,000.
As a result of our experience with similar projects, we know that if tenders were called for the extension of the Maisonnette wharf in order to provide water of a depth of four feet, which will give good but not perfect shelter, the project could be completed at a cost of about $125,000. This would be definitely in line with similar projects approved by the department in the past. I hope that the fishermen of Maisonnette will be granted this extension to their wharf without delay. This extension would provide urgently needed protection because every year these fishermen 90205-6-404J
Supply-Public Works
lose two or three boats during storms and, in addition to that, their fishing operations have to be curtailed.
There is also before the department a request for the replacement of the Lower Caraquet wharf which was carried away during a storm in 1958. Early in 1959, the Minister of Public Works notified the local chamber of commerce that the replacement of the wharf would be considered in the 196061 estimates. However, the 1960-61 estimates were introduced, and they did not contain any item for the replacement of the Lower Caraquet wharf. We now have the 1961-62 estimates, and again there is no item to cover the replacement of this wharf. I hope the minister will give serious consideration to the replacement of this wharf which is needed for the development of the fishing industry in that area.
Another fishing community in my constituency at which some improvements are needed is Ferguson gully. I understand that if the department were to accept the request of the local fishermen, a major expenditure would be involved. However, the first request has been amended and the fishermen will now be satisfied if the department will undertake an experiment and have a cut made through the sandbar in order to allow these fishermen to go out to the fishing grounds. I would ask the minister to advise us whether or not this project could be undertaken during the present summer.
The last fishing community which I shall mention at this time is Pigeon Hill. We have 55 fishing boats operating out of this community, and these fishermen have no shelter, no landing accommodation whatever. They have to launch their fishing craft every morning and beach them when they come back from the fishing grounds in the evening. This locality is along the shores of the gulf of St. Lawrence, and if the local fishermen were to leave their boats at anchor there would be a good chance the boats would be gone before morning. I know that the minister is aware of the situation at Pigeon Hill. I know that it could involve some major expenditure. I feel, however, that the expenditure is well warranted in view of the heavy production and the large number of fishing boats involved. I have been told that every morning the minister uses his canoe by means of which to go from his home to his office. If the minister were obliged to go through what our fishermen at Pigeon Hill are obliged to go through every morning he would be more fully aware of the situation.
I have here a picture which appeared in the newspaper Evangeline for Thursday, May 25. It shows these fishermen having to launch

Supply-Public Works
their boats loaded with traps. Here is a fishing boat 35 feet or 38 feet in length and loaded with 40 lobster traps. The fishermen have to go into the water up to their waists and be exposed to two-foot or three-foot waves, and on many occasions they are obliged to spend a whole day soaked to their waists. If, while launching their boats, the waves get over their high rubber boots and rubber suits, they are obliged to carry on fishing all day that way. If the minister had to get his feet wet, at least he could come to his office and in a warm spot dry off very quickly. For the information of the minister I am sending this picture over to him. It will give him firsthand information of the misery these fishermen are obliged to go through.
I am positive that the project at Pigeon Hill is not impossible. It is true that an engineering problem exists, but the engineers of his department in the past have taken care of problems which were just as serious as is the one at Pigeon Hill. I hope that this project will receive serious and early consideration.

I should like to ask a question of the hon. member who has just taken his seat, if he does not mind. Since the hon. member always maintains that he is a good representative of New Brunswick, I should like to know why he did not ask for anything for the constituency of Restigouche-Mada-waska.

As the bright boy has asked me this question, Mr. Chairman, I will tell the hon. member this. When we come to item 362 I may have a series of questions to address to the minister concerning the constituency of Restigouche-Madawaska.
We have a good member. We do not need them.

First, I think the committee would be pleased to know that the minister has recently retrieved this famous canoe in which he moves to and from work. It apparently was lost, strayed or stolen a while back but now it has been returned safely and the minister is again paddling his own canoe.
I have two suggestions to make and I hope the minister will not tell me to paddle my own canoe. They will be short ones and I will not take too much of his time. The first is a request or a suggestion-and I made it some two years ago or three years ago- that more attention be paid to the problems of paraplegics when public buildings are designed. I know the minister has continued the program his precedessor followed of doing something for paraplegics, but there are still in this country a number of public buildings which are going up without due regard to

those unfortunates. There are ready architectural plans, for example, in all the buildings put up by the Department of Veterans Affairs. As I say these plans are available to the architects who design the other buildings. I hope the minister will aggressively see to it that all public buildings will have entrances that are suitable to paraplegics. When I went through Dalhousie law school I had the personal experience of helping to move into and out of the school a student who was a paraplegic. From that personal experience I know of the problems that face these people.
The second point, Mr. Chairman, deals with your grand province of Quebec. I should like to make this point in French except for the fact that, despite hard study, my French is of the nature that has to be translated in booths on both sides of the chamber. I will therefore make the remarks in English, if I may do so. I visited several places in Quebec recently and was somewhat surprised to find that companies which had set up what I suppose you would call the company style town, had incorporated the English Canadian style of architecture rather than the French Canadian style of architecture in their building development. This seemed to be most surprising. Subsequently I talked about this matter with officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in order to ascertain whether there were any homes of distinctively French Canadian design that could qualify for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loans. I am informed that the corporation is doing all it can to encourage architects in Quebec to come up with homes of this style with a peculiarly Quebec flair. I hope the minister and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will encourage these architects to achieve something that will reach that goal.

I have had a number of petitions which I have passed on to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation regarding the construction of many of these houses. These petitions relate to such things as faulty eavestroughs, downspouts, condensation on the ceilings, and particularly to hot water tanks. I should say I have had over 200 different such cases brought to my attention.
I know that the matter is not one that is easily dealt with because it is a matter involving housing inspection. However, I believe, since the government is prepared under legislation that exists to assist in the construction of homes as a guarantor, we have an obligation to see that the standards laid down by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are observed. In the case of the hot water tanks, for instance, the argument is made that there is a guarantee in some cases for as long as 10 years, but it is only regarded by the corporation as a standard of a recommendatory character. In some cases defects have shown up in the course of less than a year. I am sure that what

I say applies not only to my constituency but to other sections of the city of Windsor as well as other communities in Canada. I do not want to overstate the case and I do not want to hurt any builder unduly or unfairly, but I am sure many hon. members have had the experience of people going into houses where the construction has been faulty, where hot water tanks and the like have been faulty.
It seems to me that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation could do something more than merely express the view that these standards are recommendatory. I realize there is an important policing job here. The minister will recall that last year I urged upon him that steps ought to be taken to avoid discrimination in the matter of any individual being denied the opportunity to obtain credit for the purpose of building a house. At any rate, the initial view of the minister was that this was a provincial matter. The minister did, finally, find a method of coping with the problem. I am suggesting to him that in this kind of situation some effort ought to be made to see that builders do live up to the standards laid down by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I would ask the minister to have this matter referred once more to the director for all the data I have supplied to the latter in this matter.
