Mr. Chairman, I intervene in this debate on the estimates of the Department of Public Works at this time to discuss a matter of particular importance to

Supply-Public Works
a certain group of people and, I am sure, to the department, as well as to myself.
I have reference to an item in the estimates in relation to the harbours and rivers engineering services. Normally I should wait to discuss this matter until we were considering that item but because of the sittings of the committee, on railways, air lines and other agencies owned and operated by the government, of which I am a member, I feel that this is the only time at which I can discuss this matter.
The minister over a period of months, and I believe longer, has received representations from the Cornwall industrial development commission for the establishment of wharfing facilities at Cornwall.
I have indicated during the discussion on previous occasions of the estimates of the minister that the committee and the department might well have given consideration to a suggestion which had been made earlier by myself for the establishment of an economic survey to deal with the effect of the St. Lawrence seaway upon the area which it traverses. While that recommendation was approved unanimously by the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, no action was taken in respect to it.
There was a recommendation approved not long ago by the same committee, also unanimously, to increase the directors of the Canadian National Railways from seven to 12. Although there was very little discussion of that matter it was approved immediately. However, my suggestion fell by the wayside.
The Department of Public Works did set up a committee to consider, in conjunction I understand with the Department of Transport, the advisability of the establishment of port facilities along the front of the seaway extending from Dorion on the east as far as Oshawa, I believe.
When the minister replies to these suggestions he might give us a detailed report in respect to what has happened to the recommendations of this committee, in addition to what is being done at Cornwall, of course. There the department has decided to build a wharf. There is in the estimates the sum of $300,000 for that purpose.
The construction of that wharf was recommended in a brief presented to the Department of Public Works by the industrial commission for the city of Cornwall to illustrate the immediate need for a wharf and deep sea water facilities in that area. That was also recommended by the Cornwall industrial development corporation.
At this stage I should like to pause for a moment and place on the record a statement contained in a speech I made on September

11, 1956 on the occasion of the ceremony of laying the cornerstone of the headquarters building at Cornwall. That paragraph reads as follows:
What I have said of Canada applies in a proportionate degree to Cornwall. Its growth in the last quarter of a century has been remarkable. Today it is the fastest growing community in eastern Ontario, it is an important industrial centre-it could become a port bustling with activity. There was a time when the wharf at the foot of Pitt street was the busiest place in town. At the turn of the century, following the construction of the 14 foot canal through this area, Cornwall thrived from water transportation. With the coming of the railways and the construction of modern highways, competition from these forms of transportation was faster and more efficient and water transportation in this area became a poor third. But here is an opportunity and a great one to regain our long lost prestige on the water. We are bringing deep sea navigation right up to your door. There is a natural harbour from St. Lawrence park to Gray's creek. Get the business, get the industries and soon a port will flourish and thrive on your waterfront. Here you will have to rely upon your own initiative. The government cannot be expected to build navigation facilities which will attract industry and at the same time develop a port on your waterfront. Here is an opportunity to exercise the drive and energy I referred to earlier.
The government and the seaway authority have confidence in the future of Cornwall. Not only have they made sure that deep water navigation will be available to you but they have selected this city as the headquarters of the seaway authority. When the seaway is completed, its operations will be directed from here and for that purpose we have erected on this site a modern and efficient building.
Even before that the Canadian National Railways had conducted a survey of the proposed deep waterway project and its effect upon the community of Cornwall. This survey was prepared by the development branch of the department of research and development of the Canadian National Railways in September, 1953, and among the many recommendations it made, the following recommendation appeared:
2. That the zoning authorities for greater Cornwall be advised to protect for industrial use, by restrictive zoning, an area of about 1,000 acres beyond the growing housing development east of Courtaulds and lying between the present Canadian National Railways main line and the St. Lawrence river.
This area, which that branch of the Canadian National Railways recommended, is not far east of the area in which the Department of Public Works intends to build this wharf. My purpose in referring to this recommendation is that, acting upon it, the city council at that time expropriated, or took an option, on the property referred to by the Canadian National Railways, which is roughly speaking, a mile or more downstream from the present wharf which is being built by the department. At this point the deep water facilities range anywhere from 23 feet to 42 feet in

depth. Therefore, there was not any doubt
that deep-sea vessels could come into that area.
I raise this point not because I have any complaints to make about the site chosen by the Department of Public Works. On the contrary, I think the question is one for the local authorities, the city and those who are concerned, to determine. If at a later date the city fathers saw fit to believe that the recommendations made by the Canadian National Railways were not applicable in 1960 or 1961, I certainly have no fault to find. I think the decision of the industrial development corporation in selecting that area, having regard to the circumstances and the time at which it was done, is perhaps superior today to the recommendation made by the Canadian National Railways. I say that because the industrial development corporation purchased a number of mills. It purchased the Canada mill and the Dundas mill for industrial development purposes, and then they got the idea of developing the wharf, which to my mind is an excellent one, and they should be commended for it. The industrial development corporation deserves a great deal of commendation for the interest it is taking in the development of industry in that vicinity.
My particular purpose in rising is that it has been repeated in the house and elsewhere that if there has been a decline in business activity in the community of Cornwall it is due to the St. Lawrence seaway. No statement could be further from the truth. The statement is inaccurate. It is one which should be challenged in the light of the development that is being carried on by the Department of Public Works in the eastern part of the city of Cornwall.
It has been stated also that the economy of Cornwall declined because the St. Lawrence seaway canals were put on the United States side of the line. This statement is also inaccurate. If I go back to history I can show that the statement is inaccurate. The 1932 United States-Canada agreement provided for a two-stage development of power and navigation in that area. It provided for one canal on the United States side at Barnhart island and the other canal on the Canadian side at Chrysler island upstream from Cornwall. The 1941 agreement provided for both canals on the United States side. The 1954 proposal to the international joint commission provided for an undertaking by Canada that it would build all the facilities on the Canadian side of the line, but as the committee knows, following the meetings that took place between the United States representatives and the Canadian representatives, it was decided to build one canal and
Supply-Public Works
two locks opposite Barnhart island on the United States side and one canal and one lock at Iroquois on the Canadian side. And Canada undertook to continue 14 foot navigation on the Canadian side at Cornwall. Therefore, there is now not only a deep channel of 27 feet not very far from the wharf which the department is building but also a canal 14 feet in depth upstream from that area.
It has been said that little or no traffic goes through that canal now. I mention this because it has a great deal to do with the wharf which the department is building. Fortunately, because of the 27 foot facilities which are practically opposite the wharf which is being built, there will have to be little or no dredging. In fact, the wharf comes practically to the end of the 27 foot facilities. This will enable deep-sea ships to go right to the wharf when the department is building.
Since it has been stated in the house and outside that because of the seaway the traffic has diminished tremendously I should like to put on Hansard figures indicating the amount of local traffic that went through the Cornwall canal from 1947 to 1959. These figures have been obtained from the St. Lawrence seaway authority, statistics section. They are dated August 18, 1960. I should like the permission of the committee to place these figures on Hansard.

My purpose in putting these figures on the record is to indicate that in the old days the traffic on the St. Lawrence canal at Cornwall was tremendous and, in fact, was responsible in large part for the 

progress and development of that community, but as the railways came into being and as trucks and all the other methods of transportation advanced traffic gradually declined. From a peak of about 300,000 tons of traffic annually, reached after 1947, it went to 183,000 tons in 1960. So there is not a great deal of difference so far as that is concerned.
It was also stated that because of the facilities that were provided on the United States side of the line tremendous growth took place at Massena, N.Y. That statement is also inaccurate. There is no port at Massena but there are two industries at a place called Rooseveltown, New York, to the south almost diagonally opposite the wharf which is being built by the Department of Public Works. Reynolds Aluminum has established an industry there and General Motors have established a Chevrolet plant also. These developments have not taken place on account of port facilities because there are none there. They are due to railway and highway facilities and particularly due to the fact that the New York state power authority saw fit to allocate to the northern New York area, particularly Rooseveltown, a large block of power. That was unlike what was done by the Ontario hydro commission which decided to allocate no power to the immediate vicinity in the international section at Cornwall but rather decided to feed it all into the grid and thus transport it for the development of industry in southern and southwestern Ontario.
As the committee knows, what has been the difficulty in the community, which is being remedied by this and other actions to which I will refer in a moment, what was responsible for the boom was the fact that during the construction of the seaway no less than $800 million was spent within an area of five or ten miles of the city of Cornwall. When the construction work ceased there was of course a great letdown so far as public expenditure was concerned and business declined. However, if there has been a decline in the economy it has been due mostly to the closing of the three cotton industries to which I referred on another occasion although I will not go into that matter at this time.
I want to come back now to the wharf being built by the department. As the minister knows, this project was announced last year. I believe that in December of last year the mayor of the city of Cornwall announced that this would be done and from that time on all sorts of hopeful statements have appeared in the local press under headings such as "Seaway City Name a Reality at Last", "Perhaps City's Seaway Dream Wrapped in the Harbour", "Seaway About to Enter Period of Adjustment", "Seaway

Wharf May Mark Turning of the Tide". Editorials under headings of this type appeared in the Cornwall Standard-Freeholder over a period from December last year even up to May of this year.
In one editorial at least some surprise is expressed at the fact that these facilities will not be started until August of this year. When the minister replies, I should like him to give some indication of why there should be such a delay. The announcement was made by the mayor in December of last year. It was confirmed by the present mayor at a later date. I believe the minister himself made an announcement. There has been an item in the estimates on one occasion and I may be mistaken but I believe there was also an item in a supplementary estimate.
As set forth in an editorial in a recent issue of the Standard-Freeholder, the question which arises is why the work is not to begin until the month of August. I think it is well to bring to the attention of the minister and the department matters which I am sure have been brought to their attention already. I bring them to the minister's attention again because I have been requested to do so. I bring them to his attention particularly because of the work that is being done by the industrial development corporation. Without any hope of remuneration, they have purchased the facilities belonging to the Canada and the Dundas cotton mills as I have said, and they are actively soliciting industries. They have already succeeded in bringing to the area two industries and they hope to be able to have another one in the near future. They are convinced that this facility being established by the department will enhance tremendously the value of the premises which they have purchased.
I need hardly tell the minister that in order to encourage industry there should not only be rail and highway facilities but there must of necessity also be cheap water transportation facilities. Those who have been critical of the former administration should be reminded that a channel 27 feet in depth was built alongside the wharf and leading up to a structure in the dike of the power dam in order to provide for a deep-water canal on the Canadian side should the volume of traffic on the seaway warrant it at a later date. These people should be reminded that here is a channel that has permitted the Department of Public Works to build a wharf and I hope a shed also in due course.
I believe the department would not have thought for one moment of constructing these facilities had there not been a 27-foot depth of water in the immediate area. The fact that there is in Cornwall the headquarters
Supply-Public Works
building of the St. Lawrence seaway authority, which houses some 150 people, and the fact that the former administration took the decision to build two international bridges there, one to connect the United States shore with the Canadian shore over the south channel and another to connect Cornwall island and the city of Cornwall over the north channel, should be encouraging factors and should confirm the department in the view that the money to be spent here is money that will be well spent.
There is a great deal more that I think the department can do, and I hope the minister and his officials will continue to give consideration to further facilities as time goes on. However, there is one thing particularly which I have been requested to bring to the attention of the committee, the fact that construction under this program announced many months ago has not yet started. If the Department of Public Works will give this development the same attention and care that it gives to many of its other public projects, I am sure the city of Cornwall will thrive and benefit from this expenditure.

Mr. Chairman, I find in the book of estimates an item which reads as follows: "St. Hilaire retaining wall, $100,000". First, I wish to thank the minister and the Department of Public Works for their kind attention in solving this problem at St. Hilaire. I should like to remind the minister that sometimes after there has been publication in the newspapers of the fact that certain works are to be performed by his department, the work is not actually performed before the fiscal year is ended. This happened once in respect of St. Hilaire, and I hope that the minister will inform the appropriate officials-perhaps if the former member for Stormont would discuss his problems outside the chamber, I could continue my speech.
I was saying that two years ago there was supposed to be a retaining wall built in the vicinity of St. Hilaire at a cost of $75,000. Something happened and the work was not actually performed by the department before the end of the fiscal year. I understand that the amount has now been increased by $25,000, bringing it up to $100,000. I am going to take advantage of this opportunity, therefore, to thank the minister for increasing the amount. However, I should like to make sure that his officials, either in Montreal or in Ottawa, see to it that construction of this retaining wall is undertaken not later than July 15. I hope that I shall soon read in the newspapers that tenders have been called by the Department of Public Works for the construction of this protecting wall.

Supply-Public Works
I do not want to ask for too much for my own constituency. However, I have a few remarks to make in connection with the needs of some of the municipalities in my constituency which can be met by the Department of Public Works.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I understand that in St. Hilaire the municipal council was planning to build a main sewer of some importance. This main sewer could be installed on the shores of the Richelieu river so that the pipes could lead to a sewage disposal plant. It might be advisable to build the retaining wall needed in the village of St. Hilaire at the same time as the main sewer the municipality proposes to install jointly with the municipality of Otterburn Park.
This retaining wall could be built by the federal government while the main sewer would be installed by the municipality, possibly as a joint operation. Of course, many details remain to be discussed. However, I ask the minister to intervene so that his departmental officials in Montreal meet with the St. Hilaire municipal authorities to discuss this project as soon as possible.
The above-mentioned retaining wall which is planned for this year extends over a section outside the village. That is justifiable because there are houses on this section of land that are inhabited all year round by country people around St. Hilaire.
It is extremely important that those properties be protected before those in the village, because the houses there are not near the river but some distance away from it. In fact, the provincial highway which is also the main street of St. Hilaire, runs between the shore and the houses; but nevertheless, the highway may possibly cave in. It is essential that the Department of Public Works take action without delay.
The federal government should avail itself of this opportunity to open negotiations with the municipality of St. Hilaire and undertake both projects simultaneously so as to avoid duplication and enable the municipality of St. Hilaire to build its main sewer as cheaply as possible.
It has been pointed out to me that in Otter-burn Park a wharf owned by the federal government is in need of repairs. I call the minister's attention to this matter and I ask that an investigation be made as soon as possible.


Since we are speaking of wharves, it might be advisable to repair the Chambly canal and its wharf pending the implementation of the Richelieu waterway project.
I should like now to refer to the Marieville post office. On page 461 of the main estimates, I note that an amount of $30,000 is provided to repair and extend the Marieville post office. Up to now, discussions have taken place between representatives of the federal Department of Public Works and those of the previous municipal council. Since then, there were both provincial and municipal elections. The municipal council has been substantially altered and I think negotiations would have to start from scratch to bring the new members up to date.
Following the provincial election, changes were made within the department of Public Works in Quebec City. Employees of the department were transferred from Montreal, amongst others Mr. Martineau, architect, who was responsible for the plans for an addition and repairs to the post office of Marieville. Someone from the department's Montreal office should get in touch with the new municipal council of Marieville so that an agreement could be reached. There is a problem, however; the property next to the post office belongs to the municipality.
The municipality is asking a prohibitive price for that property. A meeting should therefore be arranged between the representatives of the Department of Public Works and those of the municipality to convince the latter that the property which is needed for the construction of the addition should be sold to the federal government for a fair and reasonable price.
Mr. Chairman, I should also like to call the minister's attention to the fact that a pile of Fryer dam on Fryer island, between Richelieu and Chambly on the Richelieu, has been in need of repair for the past two years.
If I remember well, I was told by the Department of Public Works, two years ago, that those repairs were urgent. The people of that area are still waiting for news about that famous pile which, according to officials of the Department of Public Works, is in urgent need of repairs. That was two years ago; I wonder what certain officials of the department mean by urgent repairs.
Mr. Chairman, about two or three years ago, a retaining wall was built in Beloeil in accordance with a promise made by the former Liberal government. I honestly felt at that time that that project was less urgent

than the one in McMasterville. However, so as not to deprive the municipality of Beloeil of that retaining wall and the people of that community of the work they were going to have by the implementation of that project, I willingly agreed, without too much discussion, to let the officials of the department, whether they be from Montreal or Ottawa, make the mistake of thinking that the construction of a retaining wall was more urgent in Beloeil than in McMasterville.
Subsequent events proved that I was right. In fact, the following spring, McMasterville was the scene of a serious flood. The provincial highway which is also the main street in McMasterville was under more water than it had been for a long time. Fortunately, last year and this year, McMasterville was spared that calamity, but the danger is none the less there and, each spring, floods may occur.
In 1959-I have not time to read the letter from the deputy minister to that effect- departmental officials were suggesting that a retaining wall was less urgently needed at McMasterville than at Beloeil, even though the Richelieu channel used by the ships is nearer the shore at McMasterville than at Beloeil. Such an attitude was beyond my understanding and I never could figure out how an intelligent man could write such a letter, but it is actually on file and the decision left me no choice.
However the fact remains that such a retaining wall is most important for McMasterville. Let no one suggest, like the officials of the department did after the unfortunate decision taken by the St. Laurent government, that a retaining wall should be built only where damages have been done by navigation or by erosion resulting from navigation.
The Richelieu channel is located a few feet from the highway and surely the damages are due, if not entirely at least partly, to erosion, caused by navigation.
However the matter also concerns the provincial government. As I have said already, the provincial highway is at the same time the main street in McMasterville and it runs along the river. This highway will surely have to be widened.
This question of widening the highway was raised before last summer and then was the time for the provincial and federal governments to show co-operation in order that once
Supply-Public Works
the widening of the highway was completed the federal government might build an adequate retaining wall.
I met with the members of the municipal council of McMasterville and the provincial member to discuss this matter. And although the provincial member was a political friend, I put it quite plainly to the municipal authorities that the provincial government must first widen the highway before the federal government could build a retaining wall.
This view was approved by the provincial member and he was to submit the matter to the provincial minister of highways. I was given the indication at the time that things would be settled in such a way that this highway would be widened and the only thing left to do would be the building of the retaining wall.
Since the change of government in Quebec, I have been without news from him. I know that the provincial member is a man of goodwill. He once told me publicly before several witnesses that he was ready to use in our favour whatever influence he had with the provincial government or the minister of highways. I do not know whether he made any representations, but I hope that he is better at keeping his word than his leader and that we may witness an extremely warm cooperation between the provincial highway department authorities and the representatives of public works.
Mr. Chairman, I ask the Minister of Public Works to take this into consideration so that the federal government will at least take the initiative of discussing this problem with the representatives of the Quebec highway department.
I have said it in McMasterville, I told the municipal authorities and I repeat it here- the provincial government must first decide to widen that road. But, the federal government and the Department of Public Works more particularly must do their share and indicate that they are ready to build the retaining wall as soon as the highway has been widened. I hope there will be closer co-operation between the two governments so that the citizens of McMasterville will at last be treated with justice.
They have been kept waiting for several years. In fact, when I was elected as representative of Chambly-Rouville which in-

Supply-Public Works eludes McMasterville, I was told that the Liberal party had taken advantage of three or four election campaigns to promise a retaining wall.
I was in for collecting the hats as they say in French, to fulfil the promises made by my predecessors, but I am not going to back out. I hope I will be able to count not only on the co-operation of the minister, but also of his officials, low and high.
Mr. Chairman, I have another request to make concerning a retaining wall. I am referring to the famous retaining wall in Cham-bly, that is around the basin.
There is a magnificent basin in Chambly, but navigation is doing such considerable damage to the bank that if it should continue part of Main street and Church street will collapse, and the rectory and the church with it.
It would be interesting if the public works officials were to revise their judgment. I was told two or three years ago that erosion at that spot was not caused by navigation only but was also due to natural causes. If that is the case, it should be said clearly. The provincial government should be advised to assume its responsibilities. We should urge the minister of natural resources, the former minister of hydraulic resources, to take his responsibilities and to repair the damage caused by erosion.
I still think something might be done, pending a decision by the provincial government. The federal government might perhaps decide. Since damages are largely caused by navigation on Chambly canal, which flows into Chambly basin, about 100 feet from the shore, the federal government might consider the erosion there as its responsibility and build a retaining wall.
Let no one object that the federal government has no jurisdiction. Under section 91 of the constitution, the federal government has jurisdiction on navigation and must necessarily be held responsible for damages caused by navigation. But, even when erosion is not entirely due to navigation, it remains that subparagraph (c), paragraph 10 of section 92 is specific on that point and it empowers the federal government to undertake the construction of such retaining walls.
I should like to quote subparagraph (c), paragraph 10 of section 92 of the B.N.A. Act. Paragraph 10 provides that:


local works and undertakings other than such as are of the following classes.
are considered to be of a provincial nature, lying within provincial jurisdiction, and one of those categories is category (c) which reads as follows:
(c) Such works as, although wholly situated within the province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to he for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces.
I think that section may receive a wide enough interpretation to include the construction of retaining walls. Of course, if that section were to conflict with another power of the provincial government, we could not discuss the matter, because the provincial power has priority.
But there does not seem to be any objection, in the sphere of provincial jurisdiction, to the federal government undertaking such works. If the provincial government did object to the federal government undertaking such works, Mr. Chairman, we would have nothing more to say. However, I submit that the provincial government should shoulder its responsibilities and build itself that sustaining wall, which has become absolutely necessary.
Finally, so long as the provincial government will not undertake the construction of that retaining wall, and so long as the damages are caused substantially by navigation, a field coming under the jurisdiction of the federal government, and so long as the provincial government holds on to its attitude, the federal government may assume that responsibility and build retaining walls.
If I may, I would even make another suggestion. If there is fear of taking such a decision, if even hypothetical consequences are feared, it might be possible for the Department of Public Works to arrange with the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources that the latter build that retaining wall around Chambly basin in order to beautify the approaches to Chambly fort, which is located at the other extreme of that basin. We could then have at that place a well-built and well cared for fort, with a retaining wall around the basin limiting a park, a development which would be extremely attractive and interesting for tourists.
Since I have a few minutes left, Mr. Chairman, I should like to come back to another question dear to my heart. During the discussion on the post office estimates, I talked about the possibility for the government to

make rooms available to members in public buildings. I think I can resume that point on the first item of the estimates of the Department of Public Works, since those buildings seem to belong to that department.
The Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) cleverly dodged that issue in the house. Therefore, I should like to know whether the Minister of Public Works will commit himself and mention that problem.
That is a worth-while suggestion particularly when one considers that voters very often have to see their member, even though it is only to ask for information, because, after all, instead of preaching against patronage, when we could do some, we are satisfied with not doing any, while another government, another party which-
You have no right to say that.

Here in Ottawa, I think the situation is clear, there is no question of patronage, but, of course, the voters like to see their members even though it is only to voice complaints about some civil servants, and this is their natural right.
Hear, hear.

I see that some members are giving me their approval, and if my hon. friends opposite would imitate them, everything would work more smoothly.
Voters are right when they go to see their member. They have a right to ask him for information, to ask for an appointment, even to criticize him and rake him over the coals. Therefore, it would be most important that the member have at his disposal, in a central part of his riding, an office comprised of one or two rooms, just a waiting room and an office, to receive his supporters, while a civil servant could be affected to the reception of communications from voters who would like to obtain appointments with their member of parliament.
Mr. Chairman, these requests are important, because the session keeps us here at least five and even six days a week over a six to eight month period.
It is of the utmost importance to have in the constituency a place where the electors can go when they wish to meet their representative and there should be someone, a civil servant, for instance during office hours, not necessarily at night, who would take their messages and deliver them to their member of parliament during the week end. Part of those public buildings could be used for that purpose.
Supply-Public Works
Let us take, for instance, the case of Marieville. It would be possible to reserve one or two rooms in the post office for that purpose. The post office officials could take the messages of the electors who want to communicate with their representative.
I know that is less urgent in my own constituency since my electors can easily reach me over the week end. But since we are in the house during the week, we need someone to take any messages.
As long as the members' indemnity is not increased, they will not be able to afford a full-time secretary.
Perhaps the Minister of Public Works could refer this question to the cabinet. If he would kindly and patiently read over the remarks I have made-perhaps a little vague but useful-I believe-I would be grateful to him.
I want to thank him in advance for his kind attention, and I hope departmental officials will never again pull the trick they once pulled on the people of St. Hilaire by dropping a vote for the construction of a retaining wall which was never built.

Mr. Chairman, I do not this evening intend to complain about any municipal government or about either the Liberals or the Conservatives. I mean to recall to the minister's mind some rather disastrous floods that occurred in the city and in the district of Coquitlam over each of a long number of years, and I would like to especially recall to his mind the disastrous flood that occurred in the whole of the lower mainland of British Columbia back in 1948. This incidentally, was a flood that cost all levels of government many, many millions of dollars. As a result especially of this disastrous flood of 1948 there was established what was then known as the Fraser river basin board, now known as the Fraser river board. The responsibilities of the board have been to make an intensive survey of all phases of the river including even such matters as upstream power dams, and so on, as well as flood control.
As I understand it, as a result of a letter written by the diking commissioner at New Westminster, British Columbia, this Fraser river board presents its report to both the provincial and federal governments. I should like to read from its interim report labelled "Investigations into Measures for Flood Control in the Fraser river Basin" the following pertinent portions:

Supply-Public Works
The fourth alignment for a diversion is from the Pitt river near DeBoville slough-
I might say before continuing that there were investigations carried out in respect of many possible diversions for this river into the sea in order to prevent a repetition of the disaster of the 1948 flood. The report continues as follows:
-parallel to the main road, and along the hill foot to Port Moody. See route 4, plate 5.5.1-4. The length of this channel would be 29,800 feet with probably another 4,000 feet of channel to he dredged into deep water at Port Moody.
The area is not particularly useful as agricultural land. One main feeder road and two minor roads are crossed. This route also intersects the Coquitlam river.
A concrete lined rectangular channel, 200 feet wide with bed slope .0003, and bed level at Pitt river-16.0 geodetic was assumed for the study. The only control necessary would be at Port Moody to prevent the flow from Burrard inlet to Pitt river when the tide is high and the Fraser river is at a low stage.
Calculations of the daily discharge of this channel for the 31-day period, June 12 to July 12, 1950, were made. The total discharge of the channel for this period was compared to the runoff of the Fraser river at Hope for the same period. The comparison showed that the diversion channel could discharge 18.8 per cent of the Hope flow.
The lowering of water levels on the Fraser river, through the diversion of water from Pitt river to Burrard inlet, cannot be determined from the data presently available. To obtain the necessary data would require a long and extensive survey. The answer to the determination of the extent of stage reduction seems to lie in a model study.
I have been asked by a large number of organizations and individuals to appeal to the government to undertake this kind of a survey. I am not in a position to advocate the digging of a canal to connect the Pitt river to Burrard inlet. However, I do know that this is an ancient river bed of the Fraser, and it would appear only logical that, if this canal were dug, it would very easily alleviate the possibility of floods in the lower mainland, and especially in the district and city of Port Coquitlam.
Ever since a little publicity was given to this proposal, I have received a large number of letters which have indicated that this is not a new proposal, but that it was initially raised in the year 1910, and as late, as I have already indicated, as 1955. At that time an official board of this government recommended, or at least expressed its opinion, that there should be a long and extensive survey made.
All I intend to do this evening is to appeal to the government to express its willingness to vote a limited number of dollars, perhaps in the tens of thousands, which this long and extensive survey might require, because we cannot easily forget what the flood of 1948 cost-it was in the neighbourhood of $15 million. Nor can we forget the almost annual floods which we have had in the areas of

the Coquitlam river, which have run into tens of thousands of dollars each and every time they occurred. I have received a letter from a Mr. Cannell in which he endorses the idea of such an extensive survey. I have also received a letter from a clergyman, Reverend A. J. Griffin, of Trinity United Church, Port Coquitlam, which reads as follows:
Your enclosed letter was most interesting. All points to an exciting possibility.
A long range flood control plan is most urgent in our area.
Put me down in favour of this "canal" idea- I realize a lot of investigation has yet to be done, but as you say, the potential is fabulous.
I have also received a letter from a Mr. Gibson which refers in detail to this situation. The letter reads as follows:
I am quite interested in the proposal to dig a canal from the Pitt river to Burrard inlet. This canal if dug sure would be advantageous for the control of flood. I do not think it will be long before there will be floods in the valley, from what I saw during the last winter, if not corrected one way or the other. There seems to be quite a bit of dispute throughout the lower mainland as to who is responsible for flood control. If a canal were dug this would eliminate this uncertainty, would it not? The dikes are deteriorating and should have more maintenance than is being done at present.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, perhaps the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam would allow me to interrupt to ask a question. Is the canal which he is suggesting in aid of navigation or is it in connection with flood control?

I should like to answer the minister in this way. I am not advocating that this canal be dug but am pleading guilty to a lack of adequate information. However, I am asking that an adequate survey be made as to the feasibility of such a canal. I suggest if the canal were dug it could easily be a measure for flood control as well as an aid to navigation. The minister's department is very definitely involved because that department is the only department which would do the work if it were deemed advisable. I should like to be modest in this respect and say that I am not advocating this proposal but am pleading, with some knowledge of the important matters involved, that the government expend the money necessary to undertake such a survey.
The letter from Mr. Gibson continues as follows:
No one seems to want the responsibility of dike maintenance in normal times but, after flooding, when it is too late, someone decides something should be done.
In my experience the municipal government has always maintained that this was the responsibility of the federal government, while the federal government has always maintained it was the responsibility of the

provincial government. The provincial government maintains, of course, that this is the responsibility of either the municipal or federal government. I have been interested in this now for many long years. When the present Secretary of State for External Affairs was the minister of this department we had almost arrived at the conclusion at least to make an attempt to resolve this unending problem. This has been a problem to those people ever since 1910, when the late Mr. Kilmer, an eminent engineer, advocated that a canal be built.
Mr. Gibson goes on to say:
I understand that the pumping system should be modernized soon. This may cause considerable expense. Would this canal be a boon to logging operations on a sustained yield basis for a big part of Garibaldi park and open up the tourist and Vancouver holiday trade? There is no doubt about the commercial possibilities. This would be a help, too, in relieving the unemployment situation throughout the lower mainland.
I think this proposed canal would be a good election subject for the C.C.F. party-
I would recommend to the minister that if he adopted the proposal it might be a good election subject for his own supporter in my riding, and if he were willing to dig the canal I would be willing to give him full marks. I would not even ask him to invite me to the official opening of the proposed canal, I would be so happy at the project being completed.
I also have a letter from a leading Liberal of the city of Port Coquitlam, a Mr. Harry Purdy. This is a non-political letter. He wholly endorses the idea of the government investigating the possibilities, and being prepared to spend the limited amount of money necessary to make an adequate survey. He pays his compliments to a former Conservative opponent of mine, the highly respected alderman Jane Kilmer. It was her father who first proposed away back in 1910 that this canal be dug. I have a letter from a captain of a tow boat in the waters concerned; he is a grandson of this Mr. Kilmer of whom I am speaking.
I am not going to ask the government to dig the canal this year, nor next year. However, we do have an urgent problem of annual flooding, and for the life of us, all of us, regardless of whether we are Liberals, Conservatives, Social Crediters, members of the New party or of the C.C.F. party, we cannot, and have not been able to bind any level of government down to assuming responsibility. At the mouth of the Coquitlam river on the one side there is an Indian reserve which is under the jurisdiction of the federal government. On the other side there is Colony farm which is owned by the government of British Columbia and yet the river runs through the 90205-6-405

district of Coquitlam and the city of Coquitlam. No one wants to assume any responsibility. The river was last cleaned out in 1919. It has not been used since that time for major transportation, and therefore the federal government says that since 1919 it has not been a navigable river and its responsibility has ended.
One of the letters I received reprimanded me a bit. The writer, a Mr. Cockerill by name, complained and suggested that I am overly ambitious, that I could not expect the federal government to dig the canal from the Pitt river to the head of Burrard inlet. He asked why I did not in the first instance plead with the federal government to divert the Coquitlam river into Burrard inlet and then a few years later I could ask them to complete the other mile and a half of the canal in order to connect the Pitt river and the Burrard inlet. I believe that proposal has much merit. At this time I am asking the minister in all earnestness not to be political and not to be hasty but to discuss this honestly with his engineers. I know there may be engineering interests, not in his department, and other interests that may be very much in opposition to this idea. However, I ask him to institute a survey, to spend the $30,000, $40,000 or even $100,000 necessary, because it may save the taxpayers of Canada many tens of millions of dollars in the years to come and also save the annual ridiculous cost of maintaining dikes that all of us know are inadequate, if ever exceptionally high waters recur.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak for a few minutes on the minister's estimates on a subject which I raised last year, namely the importance of the harbours and rivers division in his department to my province, with particular regard to the construction of breakwaters.
During the discussion of the minister's estimates last year I brought to his attention the necessity for the construction of a breakwater at Bell Island. As I pointed out to the minister, that part of my constituency has a very large and very important mining community with a population of approximately 14,000 and it is without harbour facilities.
When one considers the nature of transportation and its importance to this island community it is all the more important that we stop to think of the fact that this community is without adequate harbour facilities.
A few years ago a substantial public wharf and shed were constructed on Bell Island. The minister will recall that at that time he came to Newfoundland to officially open the structure. I was given to understand that

Supply-Public Works
this particular public wharf was designed in such a way as to make itself eventually complementary to a breakwater and thereby provide artificial harbour facilities; in other words a small boat basin.
The economic situation on Bell Island has deteriorated somewhat in the last few years. There is a serious unemployment problem and there have been suggestions from time to time that perhaps some of the answers to the economic difficulties facing this part of my constituency, and this very important Dosco operation, may be some incentives to those people on the island to carry on a shore fishery. Of course, in order to do this it is essential that adequate harbour facilities be provided. If the minister's department is prepared to give consideration to the construction of a breakwater at this place it will first and foremost provide harbour facilities. Second, but also important in this respect, is that it will provide adequate mooring facilities and adequate shelter for the operation of the ferry service which runs between Bell Island and the local mainland with its terminal at Portugal Cove.
Within the last year the federal government has provided new automobile-passenger ferry for this important service. This ferry is now in operation. Again, it seems to me that we were given to understand from time to time that the decision to provide a breakwater at this place was contingent on the new ferry going into service, in other words, in order to determine properly the correct location of such a breakwater with a view to providing the maximum protection for the boat. The new ferry has been in operation now for the last ten months. Again, I am not expressing an opinion of the department but it is the opinion of the local people in the area who are familiar with the tides and the prevailing winds that the necessity of a breakwater at this place has been proven beyond any doubt in order to provide adequate shelter for the ferry which has to moor at Bell Island when it is not in service providing and maintaining adequate communication with the local mainland. When the minister replies I hope he will be able to throw some light on what the plans of the department are in this regard.
The second point I wish to raise concerns a very important aspect of public works, one of the major public works projects currently being undertaken in this country. I refer to the development of St. John's harbour. The vote for this year, which I think will just about conclude the final phase of the development, is just under $5 million. The contract for the north shore phase of this development was let some time last winter. I cannot recall the exact date, but it seems to

me there has been considerable delay from the time the contract was let until the time work actually got under way. I understand that only now is construction beginning to start on this phase of the harbour development after a delay of three or four months.
I realize, of course, that part of the delay was caused by the quite extraordinary ice conditions that we experienced in that part of Canada this year. However, I feel that not all of the delay has been caused by ice conditions. I have not been successful in finding out from the contractor exactly when he does intend really to get under way with his portion of the development, and perhaps the minister may be able to give some indication when he replies.
I should also like to bring to the attention of the minister at this time my sense of disappointment at the fact that the vote for Newfoundland under construction of public buildings is substantially smaller compared with other provinces of similar size. It is substantially smaller than the vote for Nova Scotia and substantially smaller than the vote for the province of New Brunswick.
When one realizes that the department of Public Works, which is a very important department in Newfoundland, is housed in temporary wartime buildings, when one takes into account the fact that the operations of the Department of Fisheries in the province are also housed in temporary and inadequate facilities and that the operations of the Department of Labour and the unemployment insurance commission are also carried on in temporary wartime buildings, it seems to me that the minister should be impressed with the importance of providing proper facilities in the province for the public service of Canada.
I do not think it is right and fitting that departments of the federal government should be forced to operate under most inadequate conditions. It has a demoralizing effect on the staffs of these departments. They are usually working in cramped quarters and I think it would pay off in the long run if proper accommodation were provided. I hope that some attention will be paid in the consideration of the minister's estimates for the next fiscal year to providing another public building in the city of St. John's to house these very important departments. The Sir Humphrey Gilbert building, which houses the other departments of government to which I have not referred, is filled to capacity at the present time. In order to provide proper facilities for the three remaining departments, which in my opinion are the most important departments to the province, I believe that consideration should certainly be given in the estimates for the next fiscal

year to the inclusion of an item for another building in the city of St. John's to house these three departments.
There is one other matter to which I neglected to refer in my remarks with respect to Bell Island. That is exactly what our friends opposite do not understand when they refer to the trans-Canada highway and other joint undertakings. They refuse to make allowance for circumstances such as they were when the Quebec government refused those joint undertakings.
The Quebec government was then waging a fiscal war with the federal government. That was the period of the "believe-or-die" policy of the federal government and the provincial government would not give in to such a policy. I say once again that such was the policy of the federal government.
Now that a Conservative government is in power, it has a better understanding of the situation and it is ready to discuss with Quebec and even to give it back its large share. The government is ready to let the premier of Quebec accept the joint undertakings freely.
Now that our party is in power, it is possible to discuss intelligently with provincial authorities, provided that the provincial government be in earnest.
It is not up to us, the federal members, to dictate to Mr. Lesage what he has to do.

When the Liberal party was in office, and surpluses were accumulating, federal M.P.s were refusing to restore the taxation sources belonging to the provincial government.
That is why the province for its part would not enter the joint schemes and agreements with the federal government, because it rightly contended that the federal government was using subterfuge to avoid restoring tax fields to the provincial government.
The federal level was trying to invade the field of provincial jurisdiction by refusing to restore to the provinces their sources of taxation.
We are now faced with a situation of fact which we have to respect. We must abide by the commitments of our predecessors.
Now that we have deficits, we cannot for all that overlook our commitments.
If Mr. Lesage wants the federal government to restore to him the sources of taxation, he only has to refuse the federal subsidies. Then we will see whether he is a man to be taken seriously or a joker.

The provinces must have a special staff to report to Ottawa about the execution of those programs and the government in turn must hire officials to see to it that the conditions laid down by Ottawa are complied with by the provinces.
We feel that such a situation has become undesirable. The present joint programs have had a stimulating effect upon the economic and social development of the country; in several cases, they have replaced the provincial initiative. Those programs are now well enough on the way at the provincial level so that the federal government could put an end to its participation and withdraw from those fields.

should be willing to accept that request.

You are being most illogical. You are nothing else but petty political followers, the followers of Mr. Lesage, your branch manager who is getting short of money and wishes the federal government to come in and foot the bill of his electoral promises. That is your

attitude, gentlemen of the Liberal party. If you want a fight, you will get it.
We relish that.

You are saying that on the one hand Mr. Lesage is right in signing these agreements and on the other hand that we would be wrong in supporting them. Where do you stand? What do you want? Are you for or against?
Do you want to know?

Those people then discussed with the federal government.
The federal government, the Minister of Public Works is ready to discuss conditions, but Mr. Lesage did not want to discuss. the implementation of any agreement concerning the construction of a road to resources.
