I wonder how a member of this parliament who has got into the habit of looking for the mote in his brother's eye and not seeing the beam in his own, like the member for Ville-neuve (Mr. Dumas), can explain that, as a land surveyor, he is collecting fees from the provincial government to survey the road leading to the Mattagami mine.
I refer to what the hon. member for Ville-neuve, who is unfortunately away, had to say. I do not like to attack him while he is away

he was here all afternoon-but since you want to bring up those matters, we will talk about them. I am sorry the hon. member is not here-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If I correctly understood the remarks of the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville, he was talking about a contract between the central government and the government of the province of Quebec, but I did not understand whether it was about the trans-Canada highway or a public works contract-
That is right, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: One in which the Department of Public Works is involved?

Yes, Mr. Chairman, because according to the agreement entered into, the Department of Public Works must supervise the work on behalf of the federal government which is a party to the contract. As a matter of fact, even though agreements about the access roads were between the provincial governments and the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, they come under the jurisdiction of the Department of Public Works.
And just to show that those people who are talking about kickbacks are carrying on patronage in Quebec with federal funds- 90205-6-406i
Supply-Public Works
Would the hon. member allow me a question?
Do you want to ask me a question or to raise a point of order?

No, I just want to ask a question.
Is the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville talking about an access road to mines?
Yes, the Mattagami road.

In that case, Mr. Chairman, I would ask you to call the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville to order, because the Department of Public Works has nothing to do with the access roads to mines, and the hon. member should know that those roads come under the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member made a rather serious charge against the hon. member for Villeneuve.
One moment, Mr. Chairman, we shall dispose of the point of order first.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The point of order has to do with the relevancy of the discussion on the estimates of the public works department. The hon. member for Levis (Mr. Bourget) seems to think that this contract is one that comes under the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. If that is the case, of course, it would be irregular to start a discussion on that contract.
On the other hand, the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Johnson) seems to suggest that the Department of Public Works has something to do with this matter.

The Department of Public Works has nothing to do with it and the minister can confirm that.
(Text):

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Possibly the minister can enlighten the committee as to any responsibility of his department with respect to the contract to which the hon. member has alluded.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I have not been following the argument. I have no idea what it is about. What was the name of the road?
Mattagami.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: That is a road to resources. It is true that it is being paid for jointly by the province of Quebec and the federal government. So far as the administration of the building of the road is concerned, the Department of Public Works is in charge of that.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Yes. We are in charge of the administration of it. However, the amount

Supply

Public Works
paid by the federal government is charged to the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. We do a great deal of work for that department. They look to us as the responsible party to see that the proper people are paid on behalf of the federal government, that the road is surveyed and constructed properly, that the contracts are let properly and that everything is in order. We have a very important and almost overwhelming part in that regard, although the cost is charged to the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources.

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, can the minister tell the committee honestly-he has the deputy minister before him who knows about the matter if the minister does not-that the Department of Public Works has anything to do in any way, shape or form with roads to resources. I am asking the minister to tell us precisely and he can be informed by the deputy minister now.
He just told you.

No, he tried to mix up the
whole situation. That is what he did. I understand French and English, you know.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: In other words, the hon. member for Levis does not want me to speak French?
Go ahead, French or English.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I can assure my hon. friend that I have consulted with the deputy, and I will repeat what I have said. We have everything to do so far as the duties of the federal government are concerned in connection with the building of roads to natural resources. The only thing we do not do is to sign the contract and pay the share of the federal government. It is just the same as with penitentiaries. The deputy points out to me that the trans-Canada highway is the best example of our participation, but in that case we also pay for it.
The hon. member for Levis may shake his head but it is four years since he had any part in the government of Canada and it may be 18 years more before he has again. He may shake his head but I am telling him the facts. It is not necessary for him to say to me, "Honestly now, Mr. Minister, will you tell us?" I am sorry that I have to disagree with the conception of the hon. member. Whom are you protecting tonight?

Again I ask the question: Can the minister point to any item in these estimates that covers roads to resources? I am asking the minister, with the help of the deputy minister and all the officials who are around him and in the gallery, to tell me

here in the house if the Department of Public Works has something to do with this matter. The minister has said that the government of Canada has something to do with it. Roads to resources are under the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources who is in his seat. He knows that roads to resources are under his jurisdiction. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
These are not my estimates and I have not been participating in the discussion throughout the day. However, I do understand that some use is made of the staff of the Department of Public Works in this regard and that there is an involvement in that connection.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I repeat that I was thinking of the statement of the Minister of Public Works to the effect that his department has something to do with it, and it was with regard to this that the point of order was raised.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. In the document which the hon. member for Chambly-Rou-ville holds in his hand, if there is a clause which may establish a responsibility on the part of the Minister of Public Works with regard to contracts which may be awarded under that convention, I shall ask him to read out this text. However, if the responsibility of the Department of Public Works only extends to supervising from a physical point of view or with regard to the carrying out of work, I believe that this is not the right time to deal with the matter.

Mr. Chairman, the estimates of the Minister of Public Works contain various items dealing with specific objects. But when more general matters are involved, and we are discussing the administration vote the debate on various subjects directly or indirectly related to a department has to take place, if I understand the rules correctly, when the first item is discussed, and it is at that stage, to my mind, that I may speak on this issue, as it is not an item specifically relevant to the Department of Public Works but will probably be voted under some legislation which may be administered by another department. Now, I wonder at what point I may discuss this item, when for the supervision and the carrying out of that work the Department of Public Works is spending-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I asked the hon. member whether he had a text to read, because there is no doubt that expenses with regard to the roads to resources program are under the jurisdiction of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, and those items were voted when the estimates

of that department were discussed. When the hon. member says that under the first item of a department we may discuss anything that concerns the department, I agree. However, if the Department of Public Works is responsible for letting the contracts which come under the contract and is only responsible for the technical carrying out of the work, I think the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville will agree with me that it is not in order to discuss such matters under the estimates of the Department of Public Works.

So, Mr. Chairman, I will not be allowed to discuss this on the estimates of the Department of Public Works, or to expose the underhand work of the hon. member for Villeneuve with the Lesage government; I will have to wait till next year, when the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources are taken up, to raise the matter again.

Mr. Chairman, I think you will allow me to take the defence of one of my colleagues who is forcibly absent from the house owing to illness. I find it odd that the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville has taken advantage of his absence to lay a completely false charge.
He was here a few minutes ago.
I shall prove to him, if the hon. member will just keep quiet and listen, I shall prove to him-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I have no objection to the hon. member speaking now. However, if he intends to show that the allegations made by the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville are not true, he will then be continuing the discussion and it will be impossible for me to prevent the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville from replying. If the hon. member for Levis insists on pursuing that course and if the committee is agreeable, I have no objection, but if he does, I think he is opening the door to a full debate on all the facts.

Mr. Chairman, with your permission, my colleague's argument is very simple.
(Text) :
I am going to speak in English. This is the same as the trans-Canada highway. The minister will agree with me that, so far as the plans and surveys of the roads are concerned, the federal government does not have to pay a cent, is that right?

Right.
Supply-Public Works

Then, why do you accuse the hon. member for Villeneuve of getting money from the federal government when the federal government has not participated in the cost of the surveys or plans for the road? I am asking the Minister of Public Works if I am right or wrong in that. Does the federal government have to pay a cent for the preparation of the plans or surveys in connection with the route of the trans-Canada highway?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: We do not pay for the land acquisition, but we do pay for the engineering survey of the route.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: We are responsible also for every cent that is spent. We have to approve of all the bills. Does the hon. member for Levis refer to the survey bills? We are responsible for the passing of the survey bills, the engineering surveys.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: May I speak to the point of order? Would the minister dare to say that, in so far as the roads to resources are concerned, the provinces do not make the surveys and pay for them? Do the provinces then not go to the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources with the proposal that they want accepted by the department? Does this not show that nothing whatever is coming from the federal government in so far as the location of the road is concerned and anything else except the construction of the road?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The answer to that, as I understand it, is that everything has to be approved in advance by the Department of Public Works on behalf of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, just as we do for so many other departments. We are increasing the scope of our activities. What is this all about, by the way?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: The question is this.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I have heard your question and I have answered it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: The question is this: Is not the province committed to surveying the road, preparing the plans and submitting them to the department? They have to pay for the preparation of the survey themselves?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: It is the same procedure as that relating to the trans-Canada highway. The province pays for it, proves by vouchers what it is, and we check all the bills. The federal government pays its share and it is charged to the department of northern affairs.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
If you know, don't bother asking questions.

Supply-Public Works Mr. Habel: I do know because I was discussing the whole matter with the minister of highways for Ontario, and he told me they had to pay for the survey themselves.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, since the hon. member for Levis has given up his point of order, I think I could-
We shall give you enough rope to hang. Go on.

-continue my remarks. All I want to say is that hon. members across the floor helped me to prove my point. They got the answers they wanted from the minister. The federal government pays its share of the Mattagami mine road. The provincial government awards a contract to a federal Liberal member. The provincial government avails itself of the provisions of this contract to do some day labour, to make use of patronage in the province of Quebec while we, at the federal level, the good fellows, we are paying for this Liberal patronage of Mr. Lesage's. That is what you call good patronage; good patronage with good Mr. Lesage.
Mr. Chairman, I quoted the text, clause 5 is clear.
(Text):
No member of the House of Commons shall be admitted to any share or part of any contract, agreement or commission with respect to the project, or to any benefit to arise therefrom. (Translation):
The hon. member for Villeneuve who likes to come out against patronage in other places and people who misuse public funds will have some explaining to do about that. At the same time, he may have a chance to explain what happened, during the Liberal regime in the case of the retaining walls, in Beloeil, where certain foremen were appropriating public funds, cashing cheques of people who were not working, and were making money that way-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
He might explain what they were doing with that-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
-Liberal patronage paid out of federal government funds.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. Order.
I should point out to the member for Chambly-Rouville that he may be allowed to deal with the matter, but he must show the connection with the Department of Public Works.
I believe that at the moment he has wandered far from the subject, and I would ask him to come back to it.

Mr. Chairman, I feel I have followed your instructions, for I was referring to retaining walls. My remarks were therefore, in some ways, relevant to public works.
I merely want to point out that the clause is quite clear. As far as the hon. member for Villeneuve is concerned, notwithstanding the allegations of hon. members opposite, I have not taken advantage of his absence to talk about it.
I even took the care to mention first that I was sorry he was not here to speak in his own defence.
I now refer to pages 2031 and 2032 of the English Hansard. There is reference there to the member for Villeneuve.
The member for Charlevoix (Mr. Asselin) had addressed him, and here, for the benefit of the house, is the translation of his words, as found on page 6 of the appendix.
(Text):
I am reading from the translation:
Could the hon. member tell us the name of the engineering Arm which makes the survey of the joint projects?

This question makes me laugh, Mr. Chairman. To answer it I will tell the hon. member that the department's engineers are those who do the civil engineering work for the construction of the road. But I see what my hon. friend is aiming at, and I must say to him, that as a surveyor, the government of the province of Quebec has asked me to do the surveying for the expropriation of certain parcels of land bordering on this new road from Amos to Mattagami. So, to help ease my hon. friend's concern on this matter, I will read to him-I think I might give this explanation-
I have here a copy of the agreement signed by the government of Canada and that of the province of Quebec with regard to the construction of the road between Amos and Mattagami and I find the following at clause 9 of this agreement: "The cost of these works will not include any amount paid by the province of Quebec towards the project after March 31, 1966, and in all cases will not include the payments made by the province of Quebec towards-"
And I now read subclause (B):
"The purchase of an interest or any land interest in connection with the execution of the project, including compensation or indemnification for the obligatory taking over of the land or for the unfavourable soil of other lands;"
(Translation):
You spoke illogically.

How does the hon. member for Villeneuve explain his conduct regarding the question of land surveying?
He did not reply to the hon. member for Charlevoix. He tried to play on the meaning of section 9 and he was completely wrong.
Perhaps he also forgot on purpose to quote section 5 which is indeed very clear.
The people will judge the hypocrites who claim they do not engage in patronage and who set about practising the worst kind of patronage the moment they are in power.

They favour not only the Liberal lawyers of the province of Quebec but even the engineers and land surveyors who are members of the federal parliament. They are not satisfied with cramming the members of the provincial legislature, they have to give a piece of the cake to the federal members of parliament, who belong to the Liberal party.
Perhaps, one day, the minister of hydraulic resources who is now the Quebec minister of natural resources, will know how to thank the member for St. Denis for the fine work he did during his election which he won by a narrow margin, last June, and in such a way as I do not care to qualify.

The hon. member should take some rest.
(Text):

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall item 329 carry?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I have been waiting very patiently for the aftermath of the political storm that has been raised among members from the province of Quebec this evening in order to continue on what I consider to be the estimates of the Department of Public Works. It may be true that these remarks that have been made tonight have been very colourful and that they have given us an insight into Quebec politics. However, I think they have strayed far away from the field that I wanted to go into.
That is an easy slander.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is a quiet slander, and a very mild one too, I would say.
Though you are not in the province of Quebec, you can get defeated easily also.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I would imagine it would be a very mild slander. I am quite sure that the hon. member's hide is a mile thick, and that it will never penetrate at all. I think it would not even be considered slander by him at all.
Mr. Chairman, perhaps it would be wise to continue for the next four or five minutes the discussion of the roads to resources program as it affects the province of Quebec. Maybe this would be in the best interests of all concerned. However, I wish to congratulate the minister's department, and not entirely the minister, because I am now thinking of a little clipping which I saw from the Timmins Daily Press under the heading "Ottawa Report" in which with regard to the minister the following is pointed out:
He brought to Ottawa a high reputation from his legal career, honoured as a bencher of the law society of upper Canada, and held in awe by Toronto lawyers as "the terror of the negligence bar". An embittered and humbled opponent in the house dubbed him "the man with the stiletto"; his stiletto is a brilliant, lethal and always colourful tongue.
Business of the House
This may be quite true, but tonight the minister has not had to use it. If he was going to control the debate, I think he would have had to use a broad axe and probably this is not his field.
I should like to compliment the department on the work that has been done. The engineering with which I have had the opportunity to have some connection seems to be of a high calibre; and there seems to be in that department still a carryover from the days of the former minister, now the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in which he said that we would get relatively free from politics. Sometimes it may not be wise to get completely out of this field of politics. I should like to relate one particular incident that happened recently where I think it is an advantage. I want to refer to only one instance in which I asked of the department an investigation into a situation that I thought should be investigated. I gave the department the information as I had it and the investigation was made by the engineer. I happened to be in that area and I went and saw the situation for myself. It was very much as I had been told it was. I have been informed that the former Conservative candidate also visited the area. Rather than being upset about this, I am quite pleased about it because I think now there are three people who have been back to the department and have reported that the situation is very much the way each and every one has reported it. It therefore may not be wise to get too far away from this field. The former Conservative candidate no doubt has at heart the interests of the area in the same way as have the inspector of the department, the engineering branch and I. May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member means 10.30.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Yes, 10.30.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: topic

speechtext: I wonder whether I could ask the house leader whether he could indicate with reasonable certainty now what we will be doing tomorrow and Saturday and whether he could give us any idea of what we will be doing up until whatever hour it is we meet on Tuesday evening. Perhaps he could tell us whether under the rules it would be 7.30 or 8.00 o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I will announce tomorrow night the business for next week. Tomorrow we will carry on with the estimates of the Department of Public Works. The business

Business of the House
for Saturday will be determined depending on the progress we make tomorrow.
Does the minister not expect to finish public works before tomorrow is out?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I sincerely hope that we shall finish public works tomorrow. It is now June 15.
What will we do then?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: If we finish public works early tomorrow we will commence with national defence. But if we do not finish public works in good time tomorrow, I am not certain that we would start with national defence on Saturday. I am open to suggestions from hon. members opposite.
